question: What is the symptoms and abnormal findings chapter for, and when should a code from it be used instead of a disease code?
answer:
The "Symptoms, Signs, and Abnormal Findings" chapter, found in ICD-10-CM codes R00-R99, is used to classify various symptoms and abnormal findings that do not have a specific diagnosis. This chapter includes a wide range of symptoms like pain, fatigue, and altered consciousness, as well as abnormal lab results without a defined illness.

Codes from this chapter should be used when there is a presentation of symptoms or findings that are not yet linked to a specific disease. For example, if a person presents with chest pain but no diagnosis of heart disease is confirmed, the coding should reflect the symptom (chest pain) rather than a definitive disease code. This is also applicable for abnormal test results, like abnormal blood counts or imaging findings, without an established diagnosis.

As mentioned in the source, various codes from this chapter correspond to symptoms relating to different body systems, allowing for detailed documentation of patient presentations that need further evaluation or have not yet been diagnosed (source: "ICD-10-CM Chapter 18: symptoms, signs and abnormal findings").

Not medical advice. This is an educational software project. It does not diagnose or treat, and it must not be used for real medical decisions.

[1] (coding-icd10-chapter-18-symptoms)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 18 of ICD-10-CM covers R00 through R99: symptoms, signs and abnormal clinical and laboratory
findings not elsewhere classified. Every code begins with the letter R. It is the chapter for the
state a record is in before a diagnosis exists, and almost every other chapter has a boundary with
it.

The rule that governs the whole chapter is about when *not* to use it. An R code is assigned when
the documentation records a symptom, a sign or an abnormal result and no more specific diagnosis has
been established. Once a diagnosis is documented, the diagnosis code replaces the symptom code —
with one exception, for a symptom that is not routinely associated with that diagnosis, which is
reported in addition because it carries information the diagnosis does not.

## The blocks, in order

The first blocks follow body systems. Symptoms and signs involving the circulatory and respiratory
systems open the chapter at R00 to R09 and hold some of the most-used codes in it: palpitations, an
elevated blood-pressure reading in someone with no diagnosis of hypertension, cough, breathing
abnormalities including shortness of breath, hemoptysis and chest pain. Digestive and abdominal
symptoms follow at R10 to R19 — abdominal pain by site, nausea and vomiting, heartburn, dysphagia,
flatulence, change in bowel habit and an abdominal mass.

Symptoms involving the skin sit at R20 to R23, and those involving the nervous and musculoskeletal
systems at R25 to R29, covering abnormal involuntary movements, gait and mobility abnormalities,
lack of coordination and other abnormal neurological findings. Genitourinary symptoms occupy R30 to
R39: painful urination, urinary frequency and urgency, hematuria reported as a finding, retention
and incontinence where no diagnosis is recorded.

Symptoms involving cognition, perception, emotional state and behavior follow at R40 to R46. This is
where somnolence, coma, disorientation, memory loss and an abnormal cognitive screening result are
classified, and it is also where suicidal ideation is coded. Speech and voice disturbances sit at
R47 to R49.

General symptoms and signs occupy R50 to R69 — fever, headache, malaise and fatigue, syncope,
convulsions not identified as epilepsy, dizziness, shock, enlarged lymph nodes, volume depletion,
abnormal weight loss and pain not classified elsewhere.

The chapter then turns to results without a diagnosis: abnormal blood findings at R70 to R79,
abnormal urine findings at R80 to R82, abnormal findings in other body fluids and tissues at R83 to
R89, and abnormal diagnostic imaging and function studies at R90 to R94. Elevated glucose levels
including prediabetes sit inside the blood-findings block. Abnormal tumor markers are at R97, and
R99 closes the chapter with ill-defined and unknown cause of mortality.

## Codes from other chapters that symptom questions commonly need

Every diagnostic chapter is the destination for these codes once a diagnosis exists, so the useful
direction of travel is outward: chest pain to the circulatory chapter, cough and breathlessness to
the respiratory chapter, abdominal pain to the digestive chapter, painful urination to the
genitourinary chapter, prediabetes to the endocrine chapter once diabetes is diagnosed. Encounters
for observation or examination where no condition is found are not R codes at all — they belong to
the factors-influencing-health chapter.

[2] (coding-icd10-chapter-04-endocrine)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 4 of ICD-10-CM covers E00 through E89 and takes in three things that are grouped together
more by tradition than by mechanism: disorders of the endocrine glands, nutritional disorders, and
inherited and acquired disorders of metabolism. Every code begins with the letter E.

## The blocks, in order

Disorders of the thyroid gland open the chapter at E00 to E07, running from the iodine-deficiency
states through hypothyroidism, thyrotoxicosis, thyroiditis and goiter to the residual categories.

Diabetes mellitus occupies E08 to E13, and the split within it is by cause rather than by treatment:
diabetes due to an underlying condition, drug- or chemical-induced diabetes, type 1, type 2, and
other specified diabetes each hold a separate three-character category. E15 to E16 continue with the
other disorders of glucose regulation and of pancreatic internal secretion, including the
hypoglycemia categories used when diabetes is not the cause.

Disorders of other endocrine glands follow at E20 to E35 — parathyroid, pituitary, adrenal, ovarian
and testicular dysfunction, and the polyglandular syndromes.

The nutritional blocks come next. Malnutrition occupies E40 to E46, other nutritional deficiencies
E50 to E64, and overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation E65 to E68. Metabolic disorders make
up the long final block at E70 to E88: the inherited disorders of amino-acid, carbohydrate and lipid
metabolism, disorders of mineral metabolism, cystic fibrosis, amyloidosis, volume depletion and the
fluid, electrolyte and acid-base disturbances. A short closing block at E89 covers endocrine and
metabolic complications following a procedure.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Transitory endocrine and metabolic disorders specific to the newborn are classified in the perinatal
chapter rather than here. Endocrine disorders arising in pregnancy, including gestational diabetes,
belong to the obstetric chapter. Neoplasms of endocrine glands are neoplasms, though the functional
disturbance a tumor causes may be coded from this chapter in addition.

The boundary with abnormal findings is the one that catches people. Prediabetes, impaired fasting
glucose, impaired glucose tolerance and an isolated raised or lowered glucose result with no
diagnosis recorded are all abnormal laboratory findings, and they are classified in Chapter 18 —
not in the diabetes block. An abnormal thyroid function test without a diagnosis sits in Chapter 18
for the same reason.

## Codes from other chapters that endocrine questions commonly need

Body mass index has its own category in the factors-influencing-health chapter and is reported
alongside an obesity diagnosis rather than in place of one. Long-term use of insulin, of injectable
non-insulin agents and of oral glucose-lowering drugs is coded from that chapter too, as are
screening encounters and family history. Diabetic complication codes reach outward constantly: stage
of chronic kidney disease from the genitourinary chapter, ulcer site and depth from the skin
chapter, and retinal detail from the eye chapter.

[3] (coding-icd10-chapter-09-circulatory)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 9 of ICD-10-CM covers I00 through I99. Every code begins with the letter I. It takes in the
heart, the arteries and veins, the lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes, and the blood supply to the
brain. Its blocks run in anatomical and mechanistic order rather
than alphabetical, so codes sitting near each other describe related processes and knowing where a
block begins narrows a lookup.

## The blocks, in order

Acute rheumatic fever opens the chapter at I00 to I02, followed by chronic rheumatic heart disease
at I05 to I09 — the valve damage, mostly mitral and aortic, left behind by earlier infection.

Hypertensive disease occupies I10 to I16, a short block carrying combination codes that fold
hypertension together with heart or kidney disease attributed to it.

Ischemic heart disease — coronary artery disease — runs from I20 to I25, moving from angina through
acute myocardial infarction to the chronic atherosclerotic disease that follows. Pulmonary heart disease and disorders of the
pulmonary circulation sit at I26 to I28: pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, and the
right-sided heart disease that follows lung disease.

The largest block, I30 to I52, is other forms of heart disease, heterogeneous by design —
inflammatory disease of the pericardium, endocardium and myocardium; non-rheumatic valve disorders;
cardiomyopathy; the conduction disorders and the arrhythmias, atrial fibrillation among them;
cardiac arrest; and heart failure at the end of the block.

Cerebrovascular disease is I60 to I69, ordered by mechanism: subarachnoid and intracerebral bleeding
first, then infarction, then occlusion and stenosis, closing with the sequelae category for
deficits persisting after the event.

Diseases of the arteries, arterioles and capillaries follow at I70 to I79 — atherosclerosis
identified by site, aneurysm and dissection, peripheral arterial disease. Veins, lymphatic vessels
and lymph nodes occupy I80 to I89: thrombosis and phlebitis, varicose veins, lymphedema. A short
closing block at I95 to I99 holds low blood pressure, post-procedural disorders, and the
unspecified residual.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Transient ischemic attack is classified with the nervous system rather than with cerebrovascular
disease — the most common misplacement in this area. Congenital malformations of the heart and great
vessels belong to the congenital chapter, and stay there for an adult. Circulatory disorders
complicating pregnancy or childbirth are classified in the obstetric chapter. Giant cell arteritis
and the systemic vasculitides sit with the connective-tissue disorders in the musculoskeletal
chapter.

Symptoms are the other boundary: chest pain, palpitations, an abnormal cardiac finding and a raised
blood-pressure reading in someone with no diagnosis stay with the symptoms and abnormal findings in
Chapter 18 until a diagnosis is recorded.

## Codes from other chapters that circulatory questions commonly need

Many categories here carry an explicit instruction to add a code identifying tobacco use,
dependence or exposure, split between the mental and behavioral chapter and the
factors-influencing-health chapter. Stage of chronic kidney disease comes from the genitourinary
chapter and diabetes from the endocrine chapter. Long-term drug therapy, body mass index, family
history and screening encounters all come from the factors-influencing-health chapter.

[4] (coding-icd10-chapter-11-digestive)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 11 of ICD-10-CM covers K00 through K95 and follows the digestive tract in anatomical order
from the mouth to the anus, then adds the organs that drain into it. Every code begins with the
letter K.

## The blocks, in order

Diseases of the oral cavity and salivary glands open the chapter at K00 to K14, covering the teeth
and their supporting structures, the jaws, the salivary glands, the tongue and the lips.

Diseases of the esophagus (oesophagus), stomach and duodenum occupy K20 to K31. Esophagitis comes
first, then gastroesophageal reflux disease, then the Barrett and other esophageal categories,
followed by the peptic ulcer categories divided by site — gastric, duodenal, peptic unspecified and
gastrojejunal — and then gastritis, duodenitis and the functional stomach disorders.

Diseases of the appendix follow at K35 to K38 and hernia at K40 to K46, where the block is organized
first by site and then by whether obstruction or gangrene is present.

Noninfective enteritis and colitis occupy K50 to K52, which is where Crohn disease and ulcerative
colitis are classified. Other diseases of the intestines follow at K55 to K64: vascular disorders of
the bowel, ileus and obstruction, diverticular disease, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, anal
and rectal conditions, and the categories for gastrointestinal bleeding when no more specific source
is documented. Diseases of the peritoneum and retroperitoneum sit at K65 to K68.

Diseases of the liver occupy K70 to K77, ordered from alcoholic and toxic liver disease through
hepatic failure, chronic hepatitis and fibrosis to cirrhosis. Disorders of the gallbladder, biliary
tract and pancreas follow at K80 to K87, and the chapter closes at K90 to K95 with malabsorption,
postprocedural digestive disorders and the residual categories.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Infectious gastroenteritis and colitis are classified in the infectious-disease chapter, not here,
and the distinction turns on whether an organism is documented. Viral hepatitis is likewise an
infection rather than a liver disease for coding purposes, though its chronic sequelae may be coded
from this chapter in addition. Neoplasms of any digestive organ are neoplasms. Hernia complicating
pregnancy and digestive disorders arising in pregnancy belong to the obstetric chapter.

Symptoms are the boundary that recurs. Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, heartburn, dysphagia,
change in bowel habit and an abnormal liver function test with no diagnosis recorded are classified
in Chapter 18. A few bleeding presentations are exceptions: hematemesis, melena and unspecified
gastrointestinal hemorrhage have categories inside this chapter rather than with the symptoms.

## Codes from other chapters that digestive questions commonly need

Alcohol use, abuse and dependence are coded from the mental and behavioral chapter and are commonly
reported alongside the liver categories here. Adverse effects of drugs come from the injury and
poisoning chapter. Body mass index, long-term drug therapy, family history of digestive disease and
screening encounters such as colorectal cancer screening all come from the factors-influencing-health
chapter.

[5] (coding-icd10-chapter-10-respiratory)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 10 of ICD-10-CM covers J00 through J99, diseases of the respiratory system from the nose to
the pleura. Every code begins with the letter J. The chapter opens with the infections, ordered
roughly from the upper airway downward, then moves to the chronic airway diseases, then to lung
damage caused from outside the body.

## The blocks, in order

Acute upper respiratory infections occupy J00 to J06 — the common cold, sinusitis, pharyngitis,
tonsillitis, laryngitis and the categories for infections of multiple or unspecified upper sites.
Influenza and pneumonia follow at J09 to J18, with influenza divided by whether the virus was
identified and, if so, which kind, and pneumonia divided by causative organism. Other acute lower
respiratory infections, including acute bronchitis and bronchiolitis, sit at J20 to J22.

Other diseases of the upper respiratory tract occupy J30 to J39, covering allergic rhinitis, chronic
sinusitis, nasal polyps and the vocal cord and laryngeal disorders.

Chronic lower respiratory diseases are the block most questions land in, at J40 to J47. Bronchitis
not specified as acute or chronic opens it, followed by chronic bronchitis, emphysema, chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma and bronchiectasis in that order.

Lung diseases due to external agents follow at J60 to J70 — the pneumoconioses, hypersensitivity
pneumonitis, chemical and radiation injury, and aspiration pneumonitis. Other respiratory diseases
principally affecting the interstitium occupy J80 to J84, which is where acute respiratory distress
syndrome and pulmonary fibrosis are classified. Suppurative and necrotic conditions of the lower
respiratory tract sit at J85 to J86, diseases of the pleura at J90 to J94, and intraoperative and
postprocedural respiratory complications at J95. The chapter closes at J96 to J99 with respiratory
failure and the residual categories.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Obstructive sleep apnea (apnoea) is classified with the nervous system, not here, which surprises
people who expect it beside the other breathing disorders. Pulmonary embolism and pulmonary
hypertension are circulatory disease. Tuberculosis and most other specified infections named by
organism are classified in the infectious-disease chapter, and this chapter's pneumonia categories
carry instructions pointing there. Neoplasms of the lung are neoplasms; congenital malformations of
the respiratory tract belong to the congenital chapter.

Symptoms are the other boundary. Cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, hemoptysis, hypoxemia,
abnormal breathing and an abnormal chest imaging finding with no diagnosis recorded are all
classified in Chapter 18 rather than here.

## Codes from other chapters that respiratory questions commonly need

Tobacco is the constant. Categories throughout this chapter carry an explicit instruction to add a
code identifying tobacco dependence, exposure, use or past history, and those codes are split
between the mental and behavioral chapter and the factors-influencing-health chapter. Occupational
and environmental exposure codes come from the factors-influencing-health chapter, as do
vaccination-status and screening encounters, and the external-cause chapter supplies the agent when
a chemical or fume is responsible.

question: If a clinician writes diabetes in one place and cataract in another, does the "with" convention connect them?
answer:
The "with" convention in medical coding indicates a presumption of a relationship between two conditions. When conditions are listed together, particularly with the word "with," it is interpreted as "associated with" or "due to." For example, if diabetes and cataracts are both noted, the clinician can assume a linking relationship, unless stated otherwise.

In the context of diabetes and cataracts, diabetes is known to be associated with an increased risk for developing cataracts. This could lead to a coding convention where the presence of diabetes might imply a potential complication, like cataracts, due to the effects of blood sugar levels on eye health.

For diabetes, the relevant ICD-10 codes can range from E08 to E13, depending on the type and any complications. Cataracts are coded separately, and while they can occur in those with diabetes, they may not always be coded as directly resulting from it unless a clinician specifically documents that linkage.

In summary, if a clinician lists diabetes and cataract in separate places, the "with" convention could imply a connection, suggesting that the cataract might be related to the diabetes unless otherwise specified. The clinical documentation should clarify any assumptions about the relationship between the two conditions (source: "Coding type 2 diabetes: E11 and its complication subcategories").

[1] (coding-type-2-diabetes-e11)
## The category

Type 2 diabetes mellitus is E11 in ICD-10-CM, in Chapter 4, endocrine, nutritional and metabolic
diseases. The chapter separates diabetes by cause rather than by treatment: diabetes due to an
underlying condition, drug- or chemical-induced diabetes, type 1, type 2, and other specified
diabetes each have their own three-character category. Where the record says only "diabetes
mellitus" with no type stated, the classification defaults to type 2.

That default is worth knowing in both directions. It means an unqualified diagnosis does not stall
the coding, and it means a record that meant type 1 but did not say so is classified as the wrong
disease. Insulin use does not change the category — a person with type 2 diabetes taking insulin is
still coded to E11, with long-term insulin use recorded as a separate status code.

## E11 is a family, not a single code

E11 is never used at three characters. The fourth and subsequent characters name the complication,
which is what makes this one of the larger combination-code families in the classification. The
subcategories cover kidney involvement, retinal involvement subdivided by severity and by whether
macular edema is present, neuropathy including the polyneuropathy and autonomic forms, circulatory
involvement of the limbs with or without gangrene, skin, oral and joint complications, and the
metabolic states of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, the latter distinguished by whether coma
occurred. Diabetes documented without complications has its own code ending in the digit 9, which is
the source of the frequently quoted E11.9.

Several of these still require a second code. Diabetic chronic kidney disease is paired with a code
for the stage of kidney disease; a diabetic foot ulcer is paired with a code giving its site and
depth. The combination code names the association, and the additional code carries the detail.

## The "with" convention

The reason this family works the way it does is a general convention rather than a diabetes rule.
Where the alphabetic index links two conditions with the word "with", the classification reads that
as "associated with" or "due to" and presumes the relationship, without requiring the record to
state it explicitly. A record listing type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease is therefore coded
as diabetic kidney disease unless the documentation says the two are unrelated.

This presumption is the single most consequential detail in coding diabetes, and it is also the one
most often applied too enthusiastically. It holds only for the pairings the index actually lists,
and a condition merely appearing on the same problem list is not automatically a diabetic
complication.

## Codes that commonly accompany E11

Long-term use of insulin, of injectable non-insulin agents, and of oral glucose-lowering drugs each
have distinct status codes, and body mass index has its own set. Screening for diabetes in someone
without symptoms is an encounter code rather than a diagnosis. Prediabetes and abnormal glucose
findings that fall short of a diabetes diagnosis are not coded to E11 at all; they sit with the
abnormal laboratory findings in the symptoms and abnormal findings chapter.

## The general target

Diabetes association guidance describes an HbA1c below 7 percent as a reasonable goal for many
non-pregnant adults, on the basis that this level of control reduces the small-vessel complications of diabetes — retinal, kidney and nerve
disease — over the following years. The evidence for large-vessel benefit from tighter glucose
control alone is weaker, which is why the target sits alongside blood pressure and lipid management
rather than above them.

The target is individualized rather than applied uniformly:

- **A more stringent goal**, such as below 6.5 percent, where it can be reached without significant
  low blood sugar or other harm — typically shorter duration of diabetes, longer life expectancy,
  and no significant cardiovascular disease.
- **A less stringent goal**, such as below 8 percent, where there is a history of severe low blood
  sugar, limited life expectancy, advanced complications, extensive other illness, or where the
  target has proved difficult to reach despite appropriate management.

## Monitoring intervals

HbA1c is measured at least twice a year in people meeting their goal on a stable regimen, and
quarterly in people not at goal or whose therapy has recently changed. It reflects average glucose
over roughly the preceding three months, which is why a shorter retest interval adds little: a test
repeated at six weeks is still reporting mostly the old period.

Continuous glucose monitoring and self-monitoring of blood glucose are complementary to HbA1c
rather than alternatives to it. They show the variability and the low readings that an average
conceals — two people with the same HbA1c can have very different exposure to hypoglycemia — and
they matter most for anyone using insulin or an agent that stimulates insulin release.
Time-in-range metrics derived from continuous monitoring are increasingly reported alongside HbA1c.

## Hypoglycemia is a target too

Guidance treats low blood sugar as an outcome to be measured, not only a side effect to be
mentioned. Episodes are classified by severity, with any episode requiring the assistance of another
person counted as severe, and a history of severe hypoglycemia is one of the explicit reasons to
relax the HbA1c goal rather than pursue it.

## Targets other than glucose

Glycemic control is one of several targets and not the most important one for cardiovascular
outcomes. Blood-pressure control, lipid management, smoking cessation, and — where indicated by
other conditions — the choice of glucose-lowering agent with demonstrated cardiovascular or kidney
benefit sit alongside the HbA1c goal.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on how firmly to state a single number. Some guidance describes 7 percent as the
default with individualization around it; other guidance describes the individualized range as
primary and declines to headline a figure at all, on the grounds that a headline number is applied more rigidly in practice
than its authors intend.

[3] (guideline-type-2-diabetes-screening)
## Who is screened

Diabetes association guidance screens all adults from age 35, and screens younger adults who are
overweight or obese and have at least one additional risk factor — a first-degree relative with
diabetes, a high-risk race or ethnicity, established cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure,
low HDL cholesterol or raised triglycerides, polycystic ovary syndrome, physical inactivity, or a
history of gestational diabetes. A lower body-mass-index threshold applies to people of Asian
ancestry, in whom risk rises at a lower body weight.

Where screening is normal, the usual repeat interval is three years, and shorter where risk factors
accumulate or weight increases.

## Diagnostic thresholds

Any one of the following meets the diagnostic threshold:

- **HbA1c** (glycated hemoglobin, also written haemoglobin A1c) at or above 6.5 percent.
- **Fasting plasma glucose** at or above 126 mg/dL, after at least eight hours without caloric
  intake.
- **Two-hour plasma glucose** at or above 200 mg/dL during a 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test.
- **Random plasma glucose** at or above 200 mg/dL in a person with classic symptoms of
  hyperglycemia or a hyperglycemic crisis.

A second test — either a repeat of the same test or a different one — confirms the result, unless
the person has unequivocal hyperglycemia with classic symptoms, in which case treatment is not
delayed for confirmation. Where two different tests are done and only one is above threshold, the
usual approach is to repeat the one that was abnormal.

## The intermediate category

Values above normal but below the diagnostic thresholds are classified as prediabetes: HbA1c 5.7 to
6.4 percent, fasting plasma glucose 100 to 125 mg/dL, or two-hour glucose 140 to 199 mg/dL. This
group is offered structured lifestyle intervention and monitored annually, on the basis that
progression to diabetes is common but not inevitable and that intensive lifestyle change reduces it.

## Where guidance differs

The screening population is a genuine point of disagreement. Diabetes association guidance describes
screening all adults from age 35 regardless of weight; preventive-services guidance restricts
routine screening to adults aged 35 to 70 who are overweight or obese, on the grounds that this is
the group in whom screening trials show benefit. The two positions imply substantially different
numbers of people tested, and an answer about "who should be screened" should say which it is
describing.

## A caveat on HbA1c

HbA1c is unreliable wherever red-cell turnover is altered — hemoglobin variants, recent transfusion,
iron-deficiency anemia (anaemia), pregnancy, hemolysis, and advanced kidney disease — because it
measures the fraction of hemoglobin that has been glycated over the red cell's lifespan. Where those
conditions are present, glucose-based criteria are used instead. Assay standardization also matters:
point-of-care devices are not universally accepted for diagnosis.

[5] (lifestyle-type-2-diabetes-adherence)
## Why this has its own note

Diabetes is largely self-managed. Most decisions affecting the outcome are made by the person
between appointments, and adherence to glucose-lowering medication is measurably imperfect in
practice. Treating non-adherence as a character issue misses what the evidence shows: cost,
complexity, side effects, low health literacy, depression, and simply forgetting account for most of
it, and each has a different remedy.

## Diabetes self-management education

Structured education and support is described as a core part of care rather than an optional extra,
with specific points at which it is offered: at diagnosis, annually where treatment targets are not
met, when complicating factors develop, and when transitions in care occur. It improves glucose
control and quality of life, and it is consistently underused.

## Making the regimen easier to follow

- **Simplify where possible.** Fewer daily doses and fixed-dose combinations improve adherence.
  Where a regimen has become more complex than the individualized target requires,
  de-intensification is an appropriate response rather than a concession.
- **Name the cost problem out loud.** Cost-related underuse — skipping doses, splitting tablets, not
  filling prescriptions — is common and is rarely volunteered unless asked about directly.
- **Tie doses to existing routines** rather than to clock times, and use pill organizers, blister
  packs or reminders.
- **Anticipate side effects.** Gastrointestinal effects with metformin and genital mycotic infections
  with SGLT-2 inhibitors are common early reasons for silent discontinuation, and both are usually
  manageable if raised.
- **Screen for depression.** It is more common in diabetes and materially reduces self-care; treating
  it improves both.

## Monitoring that is actually used

Glucose monitoring only helps if the readings change something. Guidance describes agreeing in
advance what the person will do in response to particular readings, rather than recording numbers
that are reviewed only at the next appointment. Where continuous monitoring is available, the same
principle applies to time-in-range.

## The review schedule

Long-term glucose control is measured at least twice yearly when stable and at goal, and quarterly
otherwise. Alongside it, ongoing care includes annual eye screening, kidney function and urine
albumin testing, foot examination, blood pressure and lipid review, dental care, and vaccination.
These are separate from glucose control and are frequently the parts that lapse.

## Sick days and travel

Illness raises glucose and changes requirements, and glucose-lowering medication is not simply
stopped because someone is not eating — that combination is a recognized route into a
hyperglycemic emergency. A sick-day plan agreed in advance with the person's own clinician is the
described approach. This system does not provide one, and does not give dosing instructions.

[6] (coding-icd10-chapter-18-symptoms)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 18 of ICD-10-CM covers R00 through R99: symptoms, signs and abnormal clinical and laboratory
findings not elsewhere classified. Every code begins with the letter R. It is the chapter for the
state a record is in before a diagnosis exists, and almost every other chapter has a boundary with
it.

The rule that governs the whole chapter is about when *not* to use it. An R code is assigned when
the documentation records a symptom, a sign or an abnormal result and no more specific diagnosis has
been established. Once a diagnosis is documented, the diagnosis code replaces the symptom code —
with one exception, for a symptom that is not routinely associated with that diagnosis, which is
reported in addition because it carries information the diagnosis does not.

## The blocks, in order

The first blocks follow body systems. Symptoms and signs involving the circulatory and respiratory
systems open the chapter at R00 to R09 and hold some of the most-used codes in it: palpitations, an
elevated blood-pressure reading in someone with no diagnosis of hypertension, cough, breathing
abnormalities including shortness of breath, hemoptysis and chest pain. Digestive and abdominal
symptoms follow at R10 to R19 — abdominal pain by site, nausea and vomiting, heartburn, dysphagia,
flatulence, change in bowel habit and an abdominal mass.

Symptoms involving the skin sit at R20 to R23, and those involving the nervous and musculoskeletal
systems at R25 to R29, covering abnormal involuntary movements, gait and mobility abnormalities,
lack of coordination and other abnormal neurological findings. Genitourinary symptoms occupy R30 to
R39: painful urination, urinary frequency and urgency, hematuria reported as a finding, retention
and incontinence where no diagnosis is recorded.

Symptoms involving cognition, perception, emotional state and behavior follow at R40 to R46. This is
where somnolence, coma, disorientation, memory loss and an abnormal cognitive screening result are
classified, and it is also where suicidal ideation is coded. Speech and voice disturbances sit at
R47 to R49.

General symptoms and signs occupy R50 to R69 — fever, headache, malaise and fatigue, syncope,
convulsions not identified as epilepsy, dizziness, shock, enlarged lymph nodes, volume depletion,
abnormal weight loss and pain not classified elsewhere.

The chapter then turns to results without a diagnosis: abnormal blood findings at R70 to R79,
abnormal urine findings at R80 to R82, abnormal findings in other body fluids and tissues at R83 to
R89, and abnormal diagnostic imaging and function studies at R90 to R94. Elevated glucose levels
including prediabetes sit inside the blood-findings block. Abnormal tumor markers are at R97, and
R99 closes the chapter with ill-defined and unknown cause of mortality.

## Codes from other chapters that symptom questions commonly need

Every diagnostic chapter is the destination for these codes once a diagnosis exists, so the useful
direction of travel is outward: chest pain to the circulatory chapter, cough and breathlessness to
the respiratory chapter, abdominal pain to the digestive chapter, painful urination to the
genitourinary chapter, prediabetes to the endocrine chapter once diabetes is diagnosed. Encounters
for observation or examination where no condition is found are not R codes at all — they belong to
the factors-influencing-health chapter.

[7] (coding-icd10-chapter-14-genitourinary)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 14 of ICD-10-CM covers N00 through N99: diseases of the urinary tract and of the male and
female genital organs, together with the breast. Every code begins with the letter N. The chapter
runs from the kidney outward along the urinary tract, then turns to the genital organs.

## The blocks, in order

Glomerular diseases open the chapter at N00 to N08, organized by clinical syndrome — acute and
chronic nephritic, rapidly progressive, recurrent hematuria, nephrotic — with the underlying
morphology carried in a shared set of subdivisions.

Renal tubulo-interstitial diseases follow at N10 to N16 and include acute and chronic
pyelonephritis. Acute kidney failure and chronic kidney disease occupy N17 to N19, and the chronic
category is subdivided by stage, which is the detail most other chapters reach in to use.

Urolithiasis sits at N20 to N23, other disorders of the kidney and ureter at N25 to N29.

Other diseases of the urinary system occupy N30 to N39 and hold most everyday urinary questions:
cystitis subdivided by acuteness and by whether hematuria is present, bladder-neck and urethral
disorders, urethritis, incontinence, and the category used for urinary tract infection when the site
is not specified.

The genital blocks follow. Diseases of male genital organs occupy N40 to N53, including prostatic
hyperplasia with its subdivision by lower urinary tract symptoms. Disorders of the breast sit at N60
to N65. Inflammatory diseases of the female pelvic organs occupy N70 to N77, and noninflammatory
disorders of the female genital tract N80 to N98, covering endometriosis, prolapse, menstrual
disorders, menopausal symptoms and infertility. The chapter closes at N99 with postprocedural
complications.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Sexually transmitted infections are classified in the infectious-disease chapter, so an infection
named by organism leaves this chapter even when the site is genitourinary. Urinary and genital
conditions complicating pregnancy, childbirth or the period after delivery belong to the obstetric
chapter, which takes precedence over the codes here. Sepsis is an infectious-disease code, and
"urosepsis" is not a codable term in ICD-10-CM at all — the record has to say which of the two is
meant. Neoplasms of any genitourinary organ are neoplasms; congenital malformations belong to the
congenital chapter.

Symptoms are the recurring boundary. Painful urination, urinary frequency and urgency, blood in the
urine reported as a finding, retention, and an abnormal urinalysis with no diagnosis recorded are
all classified in Chapter 18 rather than here.

## Codes from other chapters that genitourinary questions commonly need

Chronic kidney disease is the most-referenced block in this chapter from outside it: the hypertensive
and diabetic categories in other chapters pair with a stage code from N18. Diabetes supplies its own
kidney manifestation codes from the endocrine chapter. Long-term drug therapy, dialysis status,
transplant status, screening encounters and contraceptive management all come from the
factors-influencing-health chapter.

[8] (coding-icd10-chapter-06-nervous)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 6 of ICD-10-CM covers G00 through G99: diseases of the nervous system, central and
peripheral, together with the neuromuscular junction and muscle. Every code begins with the letter
G. The chapter is organized by mechanism rather than by anatomy, which is why the block boundaries
are not obvious from a symptom.

## The blocks, in order

Inflammatory diseases of the central nervous system open the chapter at G00 to G09 — the
meningitides classified by organism, encephalitis, and intracranial abscess. Systemic atrophies
primarily affecting the central nervous system follow at G10 to G14.

Extrapyramidal and movement disorders occupy G20 to G26, including Parkinson disease, the dystonias,
tremor and restless legs. Other degenerative diseases of the nervous system sit at G30 to G32, which
is where Alzheimer disease is classified, and the demyelinating diseases including multiple
sclerosis at G35 to G37.

The block that carries most everyday questions is G40 to G47, episodic and paroxysmal disorders. It
holds epilepsy and seizures, migraine, the other headache syndromes such as cluster and tension-type
headache, transient cerebral ischemic attack, and the sleep disorders of organic origin — insomnia,
hypersomnia, circadian rhythm disorders, sleep apnea (apnoea) and the parasomnias.

Nerve, nerve root and plexus disorders follow at G50 to G59, covering the cranial neuropathies
including facial palsy, and the entrapment neuropathies. Polyneuropathies and other disorders of the
peripheral nervous system occupy G60 to G65, diseases of the myoneural junction and muscle G70 to
G73, and cerebral palsy and the other paralytic syndromes G80 to G83. The chapter closes at G89 to
G99 with a mixed block that includes the pain categories and postprocedural nervous-system
disorders.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Stroke is the boundary people cross by accident. Cerebral infarction and intracranial hemorrhage are
cerebrovascular disease and are classified with the circulatory system, and so are the codes for
deficits persisting afterwards — but transient ischemic attack is here, in G45. The two sit in
different chapters despite being discussed together.

Headache is the other boundary. A headache syndrome with a name is a G code; headache as an
undiagnosed symptom is classified in Chapter 18, along with dizziness, somnolence, abnormal
involuntary movements, convulsions not identified as epilepsy, and an abnormal neurological finding
with no diagnosis. Sleep disorders that are not attributed to a substance or a known physiological
condition are classified with the mental and behavioral disorders instead of here.

## Codes from other chapters that nervous-system questions commonly need

Diabetic neuropathy is coded from the diabetes category in the endocrine chapter, not from the
polyneuropathy block, because the classification presumes the association. Traumatic brain and
spinal injury belongs to the injury chapter, with this chapter holding the sequelae only where a
named neurological condition results. Long-term drug therapy status and family history come from the
factors-influencing-health chapter.

question: Iron deficiency anemia sits in the blood chapter. Which chapter would an underlying bleeding ulcer be coded from?
answer:
An underlying bleeding ulcer would typically be coded from ICD-10 Chapter 11, which focuses on diseases of the digestive system (K00-K95). This chapter includes various conditions impacting the gastrointestinal tract, including complications like gastrointestinal hemorrhage related to ulcers.

In contrast, iron deficiency anemia is found in Chapter 3, which deals with blood disorders (D50-D89). This highlights how different health issues can be coded based on their underlying causes and organ systems affected. For the most accurate coding, the specific details of the bleeding ulcer would need to be documented to ensure it aligns with the appropriate classification in the digestive chapter.

[1] (coding-gerd-k21)
## The category

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (gastro-oesophageal in British spelling) is K21 in ICD-10-CM, in the
esophagus, stomach and duodenum block of Chapter 11. The category is short, and the single
distinction it draws is whether esophagitis is present.

Reflux disease with esophagitis is one branch, further divided by whether bleeding is documented;
reflux disease without esophagitis is the other. Both are complete codes, and the second is the one
used for the large majority of records, because the distinction rests on an endoscopic finding that
most records do not contain.

## What decides the branch

Esophagitis is a mucosal finding, not a symptom severity. The classification takes it from
documentation of the finding, and does not permit it to be inferred from how bad the heartburn is,
from the treatment prescribed, or from the duration of the condition. A record describing severe
reflux symptoms with no endoscopy is coded to the without-esophagitis branch.

Bleeding, where it subdivides the esophagitis branch, likewise has to be documented rather than
assumed from an anemia elsewhere in the chart.

## Neighboring categories that are not this one

Esophagitis without reflux disease has its own category immediately before this one, and reflux
disease is not assumed from it. Barrett esophagus is a separate category further along the block,
subdivided by whether dysplasia is present and by its grade; it is reported in addition to the
reflux code rather than instead of it, because the two are different conditions and one does not
include the other.

Hiatal hernia is a hernia and is coded from the hernia block, so a record documenting both a hiatal
hernia and reflux disease carries two codes from two blocks. Esophageal stricture, ulcer and
dysmotility are likewise separate categories.

Newborn reflux is excluded from this category outright and is classified in the perinatal chapter.

## Symptoms, and when they are coded instead

Heartburn, chest discomfort of esophageal origin, regurgitation, dysphagia and nausea are symptoms.
Where reflux disease is documented, they are intrinsic to it and are not separately coded. Where it
is not — where the record says heartburn and stops — the symptom code from Chapter 18 is what the
encounter supports, and reaching for the disease code instead is the error the boundary exists to
prevent. Dysphagia is the exception worth knowing: it is not routinely part of uncomplicated reflux
disease, and where it is documented it is reported in addition.

## Codes that commonly accompany K21

Long-term drug therapy status is coded from the factors-influencing-health chapter, as is body mass
index. Tobacco and alcohol use are coded from their own chapters. Where reflux disease is documented
alongside asthma or chronic cough, those are coded from the respiratory chapter and neither implies
the other.

[2] (coding-icd10-chapter-03-blood)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 3 of ICD-10-CM covers D50 through D89: diseases of the blood and blood-forming organs, and
certain disorders involving the immune mechanism. It is the smaller half of the letter D. The first
part of that letter, D00 through D49, belongs to the neoplasm chapter and covers in-situ and benign
tumors, so a D code is not by itself a blood code and the number has to be read before the chapter
is decided.

## The blocks, in order

Nutritional anemias open the chapter at D50 to D53, with iron-deficiency anemia (anaemia) at D50
first, then the deficiencies of vitamin B12 and folate, then other dietary causes. Hemolytic anemias follow across D55 to D59,
divided into the inherited enzyme and hemoglobin disorders and the acquired forms.

Aplastic and other bone-marrow failure anemias occupy D60 to D64, and that block also holds the
residual category for anemias attributed to another disease, which is where anemia of chronic
disease and the anemia accompanying kidney failure are classified.

Coagulation defects, purpura and other hemorrhagic conditions run from D65 to D69, covering the
inherited factor deficiencies, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and the platelet disorders.
Other diseases of the blood and blood-forming organs follow at D70 to D77 — the white-cell
disorders, spleen disorders, and methemoglobinemia among them — with a short block at D78 for
complications of a procedure on the spleen.

The chapter closes at D80 to D89 with certain disorders involving the immune mechanism: the
immunodeficiencies, sarcoidosis, and the residual immune categories.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Cancers of the blood and lymphatic tissue are neoplasms, not blood diseases: leukemia, lymphoma and
myeloma are all classified in Chapter 2, and this chapter's anemia categories are used alongside
them rather than instead of them. Anemia complicating pregnancy, childbirth or the period after
delivery is classified in the obstetric chapter. Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn belongs to the
perinatal chapter.

The boundary that matters most in practice is with abnormal findings. A low hemoglobin (haemoglobin)
or hematocrit on a laboratory report, with no diagnosis of anemia recorded, is an abnormal blood
finding and is classified in Chapter 18, not here. Enlarged lymph nodes with no cause established
are likewise a sign rather than a disease. These codes move into Chapter 3 only when a diagnosis is
documented.

## Codes from other chapters that blood questions commonly need

Anemia is frequently a manifestation rather than a diagnosis in its own right, so the categories
here carry sequencing instructions that reach into other chapters: chronic kidney disease from the
genitourinary chapter, an underlying neoplasm from Chapter 2, and the adverse effect or poisoning
codes from Chapter 19 when a drug is responsible. Chronic blood loss as the cause of iron deficiency
is itself coded from whichever chapter owns the bleeding site. Long-term drug therapy, dietary
counseling encounters and family history all come from the factors-influencing-health chapter.

[3] (coding-icd10-chapter-11-digestive)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 11 of ICD-10-CM covers K00 through K95 and follows the digestive tract in anatomical order
from the mouth to the anus, then adds the organs that drain into it. Every code begins with the
letter K.

## The blocks, in order

Diseases of the oral cavity and salivary glands open the chapter at K00 to K14, covering the teeth
and their supporting structures, the jaws, the salivary glands, the tongue and the lips.

Diseases of the esophagus (oesophagus), stomach and duodenum occupy K20 to K31. Esophagitis comes
first, then gastroesophageal reflux disease, then the Barrett and other esophageal categories,
followed by the peptic ulcer categories divided by site — gastric, duodenal, peptic unspecified and
gastrojejunal — and then gastritis, duodenitis and the functional stomach disorders.

Diseases of the appendix follow at K35 to K38 and hernia at K40 to K46, where the block is organized
first by site and then by whether obstruction or gangrene is present.

Noninfective enteritis and colitis occupy K50 to K52, which is where Crohn disease and ulcerative
colitis are classified. Other diseases of the intestines follow at K55 to K64: vascular disorders of
the bowel, ileus and obstruction, diverticular disease, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, anal
and rectal conditions, and the categories for gastrointestinal bleeding when no more specific source
is documented. Diseases of the peritoneum and retroperitoneum sit at K65 to K68.

Diseases of the liver occupy K70 to K77, ordered from alcoholic and toxic liver disease through
hepatic failure, chronic hepatitis and fibrosis to cirrhosis. Disorders of the gallbladder, biliary
tract and pancreas follow at K80 to K87, and the chapter closes at K90 to K95 with malabsorption,
postprocedural digestive disorders and the residual categories.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Infectious gastroenteritis and colitis are classified in the infectious-disease chapter, not here,
and the distinction turns on whether an organism is documented. Viral hepatitis is likewise an
infection rather than a liver disease for coding purposes, though its chronic sequelae may be coded
from this chapter in addition. Neoplasms of any digestive organ are neoplasms. Hernia complicating
pregnancy and digestive disorders arising in pregnancy belong to the obstetric chapter.

Symptoms are the boundary that recurs. Abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, heartburn, dysphagia,
change in bowel habit and an abnormal liver function test with no diagnosis recorded are classified
in Chapter 18. A few bleeding presentations are exceptions: hematemesis, melena and unspecified
gastrointestinal hemorrhage have categories inside this chapter rather than with the symptoms.

## Codes from other chapters that digestive questions commonly need

Alcohol use, abuse and dependence are coded from the mental and behavioral chapter and are commonly
reported alongside the liver categories here. Adverse effects of drugs come from the injury and
poisoning chapter. Body mass index, long-term drug therapy, family history of digestive disease and
screening encounters such as colorectal cancer screening all come from the factors-influencing-health
chapter.

[4] (coding-icd10-chapter-09-circulatory)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 9 of ICD-10-CM covers I00 through I99. Every code begins with the letter I. It takes in the
heart, the arteries and veins, the lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes, and the blood supply to the
brain. Its blocks run in anatomical and mechanistic order rather
than alphabetical, so codes sitting near each other describe related processes and knowing where a
block begins narrows a lookup.

## The blocks, in order

Acute rheumatic fever opens the chapter at I00 to I02, followed by chronic rheumatic heart disease
at I05 to I09 — the valve damage, mostly mitral and aortic, left behind by earlier infection.

Hypertensive disease occupies I10 to I16, a short block carrying combination codes that fold
hypertension together with heart or kidney disease attributed to it.

Ischemic heart disease — coronary artery disease — runs from I20 to I25, moving from angina through
acute myocardial infarction to the chronic atherosclerotic disease that follows. Pulmonary heart disease and disorders of the
pulmonary circulation sit at I26 to I28: pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, and the
right-sided heart disease that follows lung disease.

The largest block, I30 to I52, is other forms of heart disease, heterogeneous by design —
inflammatory disease of the pericardium, endocardium and myocardium; non-rheumatic valve disorders;
cardiomyopathy; the conduction disorders and the arrhythmias, atrial fibrillation among them;
cardiac arrest; and heart failure at the end of the block.

Cerebrovascular disease is I60 to I69, ordered by mechanism: subarachnoid and intracerebral bleeding
first, then infarction, then occlusion and stenosis, closing with the sequelae category for
deficits persisting after the event.

Diseases of the arteries, arterioles and capillaries follow at I70 to I79 — atherosclerosis
identified by site, aneurysm and dissection, peripheral arterial disease. Veins, lymphatic vessels
and lymph nodes occupy I80 to I89: thrombosis and phlebitis, varicose veins, lymphedema. A short
closing block at I95 to I99 holds low blood pressure, post-procedural disorders, and the
unspecified residual.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Transient ischemic attack is classified with the nervous system rather than with cerebrovascular
disease — the most common misplacement in this area. Congenital malformations of the heart and great
vessels belong to the congenital chapter, and stay there for an adult. Circulatory disorders
complicating pregnancy or childbirth are classified in the obstetric chapter. Giant cell arteritis
and the systemic vasculitides sit with the connective-tissue disorders in the musculoskeletal
chapter.

Symptoms are the other boundary: chest pain, palpitations, an abnormal cardiac finding and a raised
blood-pressure reading in someone with no diagnosis stay with the symptoms and abnormal findings in
Chapter 18 until a diagnosis is recorded.

## Codes from other chapters that circulatory questions commonly need

Many categories here carry an explicit instruction to add a code identifying tobacco use,
dependence or exposure, split between the mental and behavioral chapter and the
factors-influencing-health chapter. Stage of chronic kidney disease comes from the genitourinary
chapter and diabetes from the endocrine chapter. Long-term drug therapy, body mass index, family
history and screening encounters all come from the factors-influencing-health chapter.

[5] (coding-type-2-diabetes-e11)
## The category

Type 2 diabetes mellitus is E11 in ICD-10-CM, in Chapter 4, endocrine, nutritional and metabolic
diseases. The chapter separates diabetes by cause rather than by treatment: diabetes due to an
underlying condition, drug- or chemical-induced diabetes, type 1, type 2, and other specified
diabetes each have their own three-character category. Where the record says only "diabetes
mellitus" with no type stated, the classification defaults to type 2.

That default is worth knowing in both directions. It means an unqualified diagnosis does not stall
the coding, and it means a record that meant type 1 but did not say so is classified as the wrong
disease. Insulin use does not change the category — a person with type 2 diabetes taking insulin is
still coded to E11, with long-term insulin use recorded as a separate status code.

## E11 is a family, not a single code

E11 is never used at three characters. The fourth and subsequent characters name the complication,
which is what makes this one of the larger combination-code families in the classification. The
subcategories cover kidney involvement, retinal involvement subdivided by severity and by whether
macular edema is present, neuropathy including the polyneuropathy and autonomic forms, circulatory
involvement of the limbs with or without gangrene, skin, oral and joint complications, and the
metabolic states of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, the latter distinguished by whether coma
occurred. Diabetes documented without complications has its own code ending in the digit 9, which is
the source of the frequently quoted E11.9.

Several of these still require a second code. Diabetic chronic kidney disease is paired with a code
for the stage of kidney disease; a diabetic foot ulcer is paired with a code giving its site and
depth. The combination code names the association, and the additional code carries the detail.

## The "with" convention

The reason this family works the way it does is a general convention rather than a diabetes rule.
Where the alphabetic index links two conditions with the word "with", the classification reads that
as "associated with" or "due to" and presumes the relationship, without requiring the record to
state it explicitly. A record listing type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease is therefore coded
as diabetic kidney disease unless the documentation says the two are unrelated.

This presumption is the single most consequential detail in coding diabetes, and it is also the one
most often applied too enthusiastically. It holds only for the pairings the index actually lists,
and a condition merely appearing on the same problem list is not automatically a diabetic
complication.

## Codes that commonly accompany E11

Long-term use of insulin, of injectable non-insulin agents, and of oral glucose-lowering drugs each
have distinct status codes, and body mass index has its own set. Screening for diabetes in someone
without symptoms is an encounter code rather than a diagnosis. Prediabetes and abnormal glucose
findings that fall short of a diabetes diagnosis are not coded to E11 at all; they sit with the
abnormal laboratory findings in the symptoms and abnormal findings chapter.

question: When one code already covers both a condition and its manifestation, is it wrong to add a second code for the manifestation?
answer:
According to the coding guidelines based on the ICD-10-CM system, whether you can include an additional code for manifestations depends on the specifics of the codes in question. The general principles are as follows:

1. **Combination Codes**: If a combination code exists that captures both the condition and its manifestation, this code should be used instead of separate codes. The combination code is intended to represent the association between the two conditions in one code.

2. **Excludes1 vs. Excludes2**: The guidelines differentiate between two types of exclusions. An **Excludes1** note means that two conditions cannot be reported together under any circumstances. In contrast, an **Excludes2** note allows for the possibility that both conditions can be present and reported separately.

3. **Additional Codes**: The guidance allows for the use of an additional code when specified by certain codes, especially when further detail about the manifestation is required. This is noted with phrases like **"Code first"** or **"Use additional code,"** which guides the sequence and determines how codes may be combined.

As such, adding a second code for a manifestation when there is already a code covering both would depend on whether the existing code has an Excludes1 or Excludes2 note, and whether an additional code is warranted or specified for that context.

For more detailed contexts on how to apply these guidelines, refer to the passages from the sources such as the "ICD-10-CM code structure and conventions" document.

[1] (coding-icd10-cm-code-structure-and-conventions)
## What a code looks like

An ICD-10-CM code is three to seven characters long. The first character is a letter, the second is
a digit, and the remaining characters may be either. A decimal point follows the first three
characters when more follow, so I10 has no decimal and E11.9 has one.

The three-character form is the category. Characters four and five add detail — cause, anatomical
site, severity — and character six frequently carries laterality, where right, left and unspecified
are three different codes rather than one code with a note. A seventh character, where a category
uses one, records something about the encounter rather than about the disease: for injuries it
distinguishes initial treatment, subsequent treatment and sequela.

Most categories are not valid at three characters. A code has to be carried to its full length for
the category it belongs to, and a category that requires a seventh character requires it even when
the intervening characters are empty — which is what the placeholder X exists for, holding a
position open so the seventh character lands in the seventh place.

## The two-step lookup

A code is found in the Alphabetic Index and then verified in the Tabular List. Skipping the second
step is the most common way to arrive at a wrong code, because the index does not carry the
instructional notes and the tabular list does. The tabular list governs.

## The instructional notes

**Excludes1** means "not coded here" in the strong sense: the two conditions cannot both be present,
and the codes are never reported together. **Excludes2** is the weaker one: the excluded condition
is not part of the code above it, but a person can have both, and both may be reported. The two look
alike on the page and mean opposite things about whether a second code is permitted.

**Code first** and **use additional code** appear as a pair and fix sequencing: an underlying
condition is reported before its manifestation. **Code also** signals that two codes are needed
without dictating which comes first.

**Combination codes** carry two conditions, or a condition and a complication, in one code. Where a
combination code exists it is used instead of the separate codes, which is why a family such as
diabetes appears so large.

## "With", and the presumption it creates

Where the Alphabetic Index links two conditions with the word "with", the classification reads it as
"associated with" or "due to" and presumes the relationship without requiring the record to state
it. The presumption holds only for the pairings the index actually lists, and it is overridden when
the documentation says the two are unrelated.

## Unspecified codes, NEC and NOS

**NEC**, not elsewhere classifiable, means the condition is specified but the classification has no
distinct code for it. **NOS**, not otherwise specified, means the documentation was not specific.
The distinction matters because an unspecified code is a statement about the record rather than
about the person, and it remains a valid code: where the documentation genuinely does not support
more detail, the unspecified code is the correct one, and inferring detail the record does not
contain is the error the convention exists to prevent.

## The category

Type 2 diabetes mellitus is E11 in ICD-10-CM, in Chapter 4, endocrine, nutritional and metabolic
diseases. The chapter separates diabetes by cause rather than by treatment: diabetes due to an
underlying condition, drug- or chemical-induced diabetes, type 1, type 2, and other specified
diabetes each have their own three-character category. Where the record says only "diabetes
mellitus" with no type stated, the classification defaults to type 2.

That default is worth knowing in both directions. It means an unqualified diagnosis does not stall
the coding, and it means a record that meant type 1 but did not say so is classified as the wrong
disease. Insulin use does not change the category — a person with type 2 diabetes taking insulin is
still coded to E11, with long-term insulin use recorded as a separate status code.

## E11 is a family, not a single code

E11 is never used at three characters. The fourth and subsequent characters name the complication,
which is what makes this one of the larger combination-code families in the classification. The
subcategories cover kidney involvement, retinal involvement subdivided by severity and by whether
macular edema is present, neuropathy including the polyneuropathy and autonomic forms, circulatory
involvement of the limbs with or without gangrene, skin, oral and joint complications, and the
metabolic states of hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, the latter distinguished by whether coma
occurred. Diabetes documented without complications has its own code ending in the digit 9, which is
the source of the frequently quoted E11.9.

Several of these still require a second code. Diabetic chronic kidney disease is paired with a code
for the stage of kidney disease; a diabetic foot ulcer is paired with a code giving its site and
depth. The combination code names the association, and the additional code carries the detail.

## The "with" convention

The reason this family works the way it does is a general convention rather than a diabetes rule.
Where the alphabetic index links two conditions with the word "with", the classification reads that
as "associated with" or "due to" and presumes the relationship, without requiring the record to
state it explicitly. A record listing type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease is therefore coded
as diabetic kidney disease unless the documentation says the two are unrelated.

This presumption is the single most consequential detail in coding diabetes, and it is also the one
most often applied too enthusiastically. It holds only for the pairings the index actually lists,
and a condition merely appearing on the same problem list is not automatically a diabetic
complication.

## Codes that commonly accompany E11

Long-term use of insulin, of injectable non-insulin agents, and of oral glucose-lowering drugs each
have distinct status codes, and body mass index has its own set. Screening for diabetes in someone
without symptoms is an encounter code rather than a diagnosis. Prediabetes and abnormal glucose
findings that fall short of a diabetes diagnosis are not coded to E11 at all; they sit with the
abnormal laboratory findings in the symptoms and abnormal findings chapter.

[3] (coding-icd10-chapter-03-blood)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 3 of ICD-10-CM covers D50 through D89: diseases of the blood and blood-forming organs, and
certain disorders involving the immune mechanism. It is the smaller half of the letter D. The first
part of that letter, D00 through D49, belongs to the neoplasm chapter and covers in-situ and benign
tumors, so a D code is not by itself a blood code and the number has to be read before the chapter
is decided.

## The blocks, in order

Nutritional anemias open the chapter at D50 to D53, with iron-deficiency anemia (anaemia) at D50
first, then the deficiencies of vitamin B12 and folate, then other dietary causes. Hemolytic anemias follow across D55 to D59,
divided into the inherited enzyme and hemoglobin disorders and the acquired forms.

Aplastic and other bone-marrow failure anemias occupy D60 to D64, and that block also holds the
residual category for anemias attributed to another disease, which is where anemia of chronic
disease and the anemia accompanying kidney failure are classified.

Coagulation defects, purpura and other hemorrhagic conditions run from D65 to D69, covering the
inherited factor deficiencies, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and the platelet disorders.
Other diseases of the blood and blood-forming organs follow at D70 to D77 — the white-cell
disorders, spleen disorders, and methemoglobinemia among them — with a short block at D78 for
complications of a procedure on the spleen.

The chapter closes at D80 to D89 with certain disorders involving the immune mechanism: the
immunodeficiencies, sarcoidosis, and the residual immune categories.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Cancers of the blood and lymphatic tissue are neoplasms, not blood diseases: leukemia, lymphoma and
myeloma are all classified in Chapter 2, and this chapter's anemia categories are used alongside
them rather than instead of them. Anemia complicating pregnancy, childbirth or the period after
delivery is classified in the obstetric chapter. Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn belongs to the
perinatal chapter.

The boundary that matters most in practice is with abnormal findings. A low hemoglobin (haemoglobin)
or hematocrit on a laboratory report, with no diagnosis of anemia recorded, is an abnormal blood
finding and is classified in Chapter 18, not here. Enlarged lymph nodes with no cause established
are likewise a sign rather than a disease. These codes move into Chapter 3 only when a diagnosis is
documented.

## Codes from other chapters that blood questions commonly need

Anemia is frequently a manifestation rather than a diagnosis in its own right, so the categories
here carry sequencing instructions that reach into other chapters: chronic kidney disease from the
genitourinary chapter, an underlying neoplasm from Chapter 2, and the adverse effect or poisoning
codes from Chapter 19 when a drug is responsible. Chronic blood loss as the cause of iron deficiency
is itself coded from whichever chapter owns the bleeding site. Long-term drug therapy, dietary
counseling encounters and family history all come from the factors-influencing-health chapter.

[4] (coding-icd10-cm-versus-who-icd10)
## Two things share one name

ICD-10 is the World Health Organization's international classification of diseases, used across
countries chiefly for mortality and morbidity statistics. ICD-10-CM is the United States clinical
modification of it, developed and maintained by the National Center for Health Statistics, and it is
what US diagnosis coding actually uses.

The relationship is one of extension rather than translation. The clinical modification keeps the
chapter structure, the letter ranges and most of the three-character categories of the international
version, and then subdivides them much further. A question answered from a WHO ICD-10 reference can
therefore be right about the chapter and wrong about the code.

## What the modification adds

Three additions account for most of the difference in size.

**Laterality.** A large number of categories distinguish right, left, bilateral and unspecified,
which the international version generally does not. This alone multiplies the site-specific
categories in the musculoskeletal and injury chapters.

**Seventh characters.** Injuries, and some obstetric and other categories, carry a character
recording the episode of care rather than anything about the condition — initial encounter,
subsequent encounter, sequela — so one injury generates several valid codes across an episode.

**Greater clinical detail.** Severity, acuteness, laterality and complication status are pushed into
the code itself rather than left to a separate field, and combination codes fold pairs of conditions
together. The diabetes and asthma categories are the clearest examples.

## Procedures are a separate system

The clinical modification covers diagnoses only. Inpatient hospital procedures are coded in
ICD-10-PCS, a structurally unrelated system maintained by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid
Services in which every code is seven characters and each position carries a fixed meaning. Neither
the WHO classification nor the diagnosis modification contains it, and outpatient procedure coding
in the US uses a different system again.

## Updates, and what that means for a stored answer

The clinical modification is revised on an annual cycle, with changes taking effect at the start of
the federal fiscal year on October 1. Categories are added, subdivided and occasionally retired, so
a code that was valid in one year may not be valid in another. Any stored or cached code answer
carries an implicit date, and a lookup against a current file is the only thing that settles
whether a code is still valid.

## Other national modifications, and ICD-11

Several other countries maintain their own clinical modifications of the same international
classification, with their own subdivisions, so "the ICD-10 code" is an underspecified phrase
without a country attached. The World Health Organization has since released ICD-11, which is a
different classification with a different structure rather than a further revision of this one; the
United States has not adopted it for diagnosis coding, and codes do not carry across between them.

[5] (coding-copd-j44)
## The category

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is J44 in ICD-10-CM, in Chapter 10, among the chronic lower
respiratory diseases. Unlike the asthma category beside it, J44 has no severity axis. What its
fourth character records is whether a complication is present at this encounter.

Three subdivisions carry most of the work: the disease with an acute lower respiratory infection,
the disease with an acute exacerbation, and the disease without either, which is the unspecified
code used for a stable presentation. The category also carries subdivisions for other specified
forms.

## The two complication codes are not alternatives

This is the detail that distinguishes J44 from most complication-bearing categories. An infection
and an exacerbation are different events, and someone can have both at once. Where both are
documented, both codes are reported — the classification does not treat the pair as mutually
exclusive the way asthma treats exacerbation and status asthmaticus.

The infection code also does not name the infection. It records that one is present, and a second
code identifying the organism or the specific infection is reported in addition, from whichever
category owns it. Pneumonia accompanying the disease is coded that way rather than being absorbed.

## What the category includes and what sits beside it

The category takes in the overlapping descriptions that clinical records use for the same disease —
chronic obstructive bronchitis, chronic bronchitis with emphysema, chronic obstructive asthma.
Emphysema without chronic bronchitis has its own category, as do simple and mucopurulent chronic
bronchitis and bronchitis not specified as acute or chronic; those are neighbors in the same block,
not subdivisions of this one.

Where asthma is documented alongside, this category carries an instruction to add a code identifying
the type of asthma, so both appear.

## Respiratory failure, and sequencing

Acute or chronic respiratory failure is a separate category at the end of the chapter and is
reported in addition when documented. Which of the two is sequenced first depends on the
circumstances of the encounter rather than on a fixed rule, and it is a sequencing question the
record has to answer.

## Codes that commonly accompany J44

The category carries an explicit instruction to add a code identifying tobacco dependence, use,
exposure or a past history of use, and in practice one of those accompanies most records here.
Occupational or environmental exposure is coded from the factors-influencing-health chapter, with
the external-cause chapter naming the agent. Long-term oxygen use and long-term drug therapy are
status codes. Shortness of breath, cough and sputum production are symptoms intrinsic to the disease
and are not coded separately once it is documented.

question: If someone has COPD and an exacerbation, is that one code or two?
answer:
A COPD exacerbation is classified under the same code for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and will have an additional code if there are complications, such as an infection. The primary code for COPD is **J44**. 

Exacerbations and infections are distinct events, and if both are documented, both codes should be reported. This means that having a COPD exacerbation does not replace the requirement to code for existing and relevant conditions. Therefore, when documenting, it is common to use one code for COPD (J44) and another for any complications, like an infection, if present. 

In summary, there is not just one code; the classification allows for multiple codes to accurately represent the patient's condition (from the document "Coding chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: J44 and its two complication codes").
