[2] (coding-asthma-j45)
## The category and its two axes

Asthma is J45 in ICD-10-CM, in Chapter 10, diseases of the respiratory system. The category is never
used at three characters, and what fills the remaining ones is two independent axes crossed with
each other.

The first axis is severity, expressed in the classification's own vocabulary rather than the
patient's: mild intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent and severe persistent, plus an
"other and unspecified" branch for asthma documented without a severity level. The second axis is
the state of the disease at this encounter: uncomplicated, with acute exacerbation, or with status
asthmaticus.

Every combination of the two exists as a code. That is the whole shape of the category, and it is
why asthma questions so often reduce to two lookups rather than one.

## Exacerbation and status asthmaticus are exclusive

The two are alternatives, not a scale that can be climbed within a single code. Status asthmaticus
describes an attack that has not responded to treatment, and where it is documented the code says
status asthmaticus and does not also say acute exacerbation. Choosing between them is a
documentation question, not a clinical judgment the coder makes.

## The unspecified branch, and what it costs

Asthma documented with no severity stated is coded to the unspecified branch, which remains valid
and is frequently the only supportable choice. The classification does not permit severity to be
inferred from the treatment recorded, from a peak-flow value, or from how the condition is described
elsewhere in the chart. Where severity is not documented, unspecified is the correct code rather
than a fallback.

## Named variants inside the category

Two variants sit at the far end of the category with their own codes rather than in the severity
grid: exercise-induced bronchospasm and cough variant asthma. Occupational asthma attributed to an
identified agent is classified with the lung diseases due to external agents instead of here, and
the agent is named by an external-cause code.

## Asthma alongside chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

Where both are documented, the chronic obstructive pulmonary disease category carries an instruction
to add a code from J45 identifying the type of asthma, so the two are reported together rather than
one being chosen over the other. The reverse is not true: an asthma code alone does not imply the
other condition.

## Codes that commonly accompany J45

Tobacco is the standard companion. The category carries an explicit instruction to add a code
identifying tobacco dependence, use, exposure or a past history of use, and those live in the mental
and behavioral chapter and the factors-influencing-health chapter respectively. Allergic rhinitis
has its own category in the same chapter and is reported alongside rather than folded in. Wheeze,
cough and shortness of breath are symptoms and are not coded when asthma is documented, because they
are intrinsic to it.

[3] (coding-icd10-chapter-10-respiratory)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 10 of ICD-10-CM covers J00 through J99, diseases of the respiratory system from the nose to
the pleura. Every code begins with the letter J. The chapter opens with the infections, ordered
roughly from the upper airway downward, then moves to the chronic airway diseases, then to lung
damage caused from outside the body.

## The blocks, in order

Acute upper respiratory infections occupy J00 to J06 — the common cold, sinusitis, pharyngitis,
tonsillitis, laryngitis and the categories for infections of multiple or unspecified upper sites.
Influenza and pneumonia follow at J09 to J18, with influenza divided by whether the virus was
identified and, if so, which kind, and pneumonia divided by causative organism. Other acute lower
respiratory infections, including acute bronchitis and bronchiolitis, sit at J20 to J22.

Other diseases of the upper respiratory tract occupy J30 to J39, covering allergic rhinitis, chronic
sinusitis, nasal polyps and the vocal cord and laryngeal disorders.

Chronic lower respiratory diseases are the block most questions land in, at J40 to J47. Bronchitis
not specified as acute or chronic opens it, followed by chronic bronchitis, emphysema, chronic
obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma and bronchiectasis in that order.

Lung diseases due to external agents follow at J60 to J70 — the pneumoconioses, hypersensitivity
pneumonitis, chemical and radiation injury, and aspiration pneumonitis. Other respiratory diseases
principally affecting the interstitium occupy J80 to J84, which is where acute respiratory distress
syndrome and pulmonary fibrosis are classified. Suppurative and necrotic conditions of the lower
respiratory tract sit at J85 to J86, diseases of the pleura at J90 to J94, and intraoperative and
postprocedural respiratory complications at J95. The chapter closes at J96 to J99 with respiratory
failure and the residual categories.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Obstructive sleep apnea (apnoea) is classified with the nervous system, not here, which surprises
people who expect it beside the other breathing disorders. Pulmonary embolism and pulmonary
hypertension are circulatory disease. Tuberculosis and most other specified infections named by
organism are classified in the infectious-disease chapter, and this chapter's pneumonia categories
carry instructions pointing there. Neoplasms of the lung are neoplasms; congenital malformations of
the respiratory tract belong to the congenital chapter.

Symptoms are the other boundary. Cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, hemoptysis, hypoxemia,
abnormal breathing and an abnormal chest imaging finding with no diagnosis recorded are all
classified in Chapter 18 rather than here.

## Codes from other chapters that respiratory questions commonly need

Tobacco is the constant. Categories throughout this chapter carry an explicit instruction to add a
code identifying tobacco dependence, exposure, use or past history, and those codes are split
between the mental and behavioral chapter and the factors-influencing-health chapter. Occupational
and environmental exposure codes come from the factors-influencing-health chapter, as do
vaccination-status and screening encounters, and the external-cause chapter supplies the agent when
a chemical or fume is responsible.

[4] (coding-gerd-k21)
## The category

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (gastro-oesophageal in British spelling) is K21 in ICD-10-CM, in the
esophagus, stomach and duodenum block of Chapter 11. The category is short, and the single
distinction it draws is whether esophagitis is present.

Reflux disease with esophagitis is one branch, further divided by whether bleeding is documented;
reflux disease without esophagitis is the other. Both are complete codes, and the second is the one
used for the large majority of records, because the distinction rests on an endoscopic finding that
most records do not contain.

## What decides the branch

Esophagitis is a mucosal finding, not a symptom severity. The classification takes it from
documentation of the finding, and does not permit it to be inferred from how bad the heartburn is,
from the treatment prescribed, or from the duration of the condition. A record describing severe
reflux symptoms with no endoscopy is coded to the without-esophagitis branch.

Bleeding, where it subdivides the esophagitis branch, likewise has to be documented rather than
assumed from an anemia elsewhere in the chart.

## Neighboring categories that are not this one

Esophagitis without reflux disease has its own category immediately before this one, and reflux
disease is not assumed from it. Barrett esophagus is a separate category further along the block,
subdivided by whether dysplasia is present and by its grade; it is reported in addition to the
reflux code rather than instead of it, because the two are different conditions and one does not
include the other.

Hiatal hernia is a hernia and is coded from the hernia block, so a record documenting both a hiatal
hernia and reflux disease carries two codes from two blocks. Esophageal stricture, ulcer and
dysmotility are likewise separate categories.

Newborn reflux is excluded from this category outright and is classified in the perinatal chapter.

## Symptoms, and when they are coded instead

Heartburn, chest discomfort of esophageal origin, regurgitation, dysphagia and nausea are symptoms.
Where reflux disease is documented, they are intrinsic to it and are not separately coded. Where it
is not — where the record says heartburn and stops — the symptom code from Chapter 18 is what the
encounter supports, and reaching for the disease code instead is the error the boundary exists to
prevent. Dysphagia is the exception worth knowing: it is not routinely part of uncomplicated reflux
disease, and where it is documented it is reported in addition.

## Codes that commonly accompany K21

Long-term drug therapy status is coded from the factors-influencing-health chapter, as is body mass
index. Tobacco and alcohol use are coded from their own chapters. Where reflux disease is documented
alongside asthma or chronic cough, those are coded from the respiratory chapter and neither implies
the other.

[5] (coding-icd10-chapter-09-circulatory)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 9 of ICD-10-CM covers I00 through I99. Every code begins with the letter I. It takes in the
heart, the arteries and veins, the lymphatic vessels and lymph nodes, and the blood supply to the
brain. Its blocks run in anatomical and mechanistic order rather
than alphabetical, so codes sitting near each other describe related processes and knowing where a
block begins narrows a lookup.

## The blocks, in order

Acute rheumatic fever opens the chapter at I00 to I02, followed by chronic rheumatic heart disease
at I05 to I09 — the valve damage, mostly mitral and aortic, left behind by earlier infection.

Hypertensive disease occupies I10 to I16, a short block carrying combination codes that fold
hypertension together with heart or kidney disease attributed to it.

Ischemic heart disease — coronary artery disease — runs from I20 to I25, moving from angina through
acute myocardial infarction to the chronic atherosclerotic disease that follows. Pulmonary heart disease and disorders of the
pulmonary circulation sit at I26 to I28: pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, and the
right-sided heart disease that follows lung disease.

The largest block, I30 to I52, is other forms of heart disease, heterogeneous by design —
inflammatory disease of the pericardium, endocardium and myocardium; non-rheumatic valve disorders;
cardiomyopathy; the conduction disorders and the arrhythmias, atrial fibrillation among them;
cardiac arrest; and heart failure at the end of the block.

Cerebrovascular disease is I60 to I69, ordered by mechanism: subarachnoid and intracerebral bleeding
first, then infarction, then occlusion and stenosis, closing with the sequelae category for
deficits persisting after the event.

Diseases of the arteries, arterioles and capillaries follow at I70 to I79 — atherosclerosis
identified by site, aneurysm and dissection, peripheral arterial disease. Veins, lymphatic vessels
and lymph nodes occupy I80 to I89: thrombosis and phlebitis, varicose veins, lymphedema. A short
closing block at I95 to I99 holds low blood pressure, post-procedural disorders, and the
unspecified residual.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Transient ischemic attack is classified with the nervous system rather than with cerebrovascular
disease — the most common misplacement in this area. Congenital malformations of the heart and great
vessels belong to the congenital chapter, and stay there for an adult. Circulatory disorders
complicating pregnancy or childbirth are classified in the obstetric chapter. Giant cell arteritis
and the systemic vasculitides sit with the connective-tissue disorders in the musculoskeletal
chapter.

Symptoms are the other boundary: chest pain, palpitations, an abnormal cardiac finding and a raised
blood-pressure reading in someone with no diagnosis stay with the symptoms and abnormal findings in
Chapter 18 until a diagnosis is recorded.

## Codes from other chapters that circulatory questions commonly need

Many categories here carry an explicit instruction to add a code identifying tobacco use,
dependence or exposure, split between the mental and behavioral chapter and the
factors-influencing-health chapter. Stage of chronic kidney disease comes from the genitourinary
chapter and diabetes from the endocrine chapter. Long-term drug therapy, body mass index, family
history and screening encounters all come from the factors-influencing-health chapter.

question: If a note says "use additional code", is that optional?
answer:
In clinical documentation, the phrase "use additional code" indicates that a healthcare provider should report more than one code to fully capture the patient's condition. This is typically not optional; it suggests that additional details are necessary for accurate coding and billing.

For example, if a primary diagnosis code does not provide enough information on associated conditions, an additional code can clarify those details. It helps ensure that the medical record accurately reflects the patient's health status and the complexity of their care. The rule specifies this when the documentation describes a condition that is related but distinct from the primary code.

This information about coding conventions can be found in the document on "ICD-10-CM code structure and the conventions that govern selection."

[1] (coding-icd10-chapter-18-symptoms)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 18 of ICD-10-CM covers R00 through R99: symptoms, signs and abnormal clinical and laboratory
findings not elsewhere classified. Every code begins with the letter R. It is the chapter for the
state a record is in before a diagnosis exists, and almost every other chapter has a boundary with
it.

The rule that governs the whole chapter is about when *not* to use it. An R code is assigned when
the documentation records a symptom, a sign or an abnormal result and no more specific diagnosis has
been established. Once a diagnosis is documented, the diagnosis code replaces the symptom code —
with one exception, for a symptom that is not routinely associated with that diagnosis, which is
reported in addition because it carries information the diagnosis does not.

## The blocks, in order

The first blocks follow body systems. Symptoms and signs involving the circulatory and respiratory
systems open the chapter at R00 to R09 and hold some of the most-used codes in it: palpitations, an
elevated blood-pressure reading in someone with no diagnosis of hypertension, cough, breathing

contain is the error the convention exists to prevent.

asthmaticus.

why asthma questions so often reduce to two lookups rather than one.

documentation question, not a clinical judgment the coder makes.

and is frequently the only supportable choice. The classification does not permit severity to be
inferred from the treatment recorded, from a peak-flow value, or from how the condition is described

than a fallback.

An ICD-10-CM code is three to seven characters long. The first character is a letter, the second is
a digit, and the remaining characters may be either. A decimal point follows the first three
characters when more follow, so I10 has no decimal and E11.9 has one.

The three-character form is the category. Characters four and five add detail — cause, anatomical
site, severity — and character six frequently carries laterality, where right, left and unspecified
are three different codes rather than one code with a note. A seventh character, where a category
uses one, records something about the encounter rather than about the disease: for injuries it
distinguishes initial treatment, subsequent treatment and sequela.

Most categories are not valid at three characters. A code has to be carried to its full length for
the category it belongs to, and a category that requires a seventh character requires it even when
the intervening characters are empty — which is what the placeholder X exists for, holding a
position open so the seventh character lands in the seventh place.

## The two-step lookup

A code is found in the Alphabetic Index and then verified in the Tabular List. Skipping the second
step is the most common way to arrive at a wrong code, because the index does not carry the
instructional notes and the tabular list does. The tabular list governs.

## The instructional notes

**Excludes1** means "not coded here" in the strong sense: the two conditions cannot both be present,
and the codes are never reported together. **Excludes2** is the weaker one: the excluded condition
is not part of the code above it, but a person can have both, and both may be reported. The two look
alike on the page and mean opposite things about whether a second code is permitted.

**Code first** and **use additional code** appear as a pair and fix sequencing: an underlying
condition is reported before its manifestation. **Code also** signals that two codes are needed
without dictating which comes first.

**Combination codes** carry two conditions, or a condition and a complication, in one code. Where a
combination code exists it is used instead of the separate codes, which is why a family such as
diabetes appears so large.

## "With", and the presumption it creates

Where the Alphabetic Index links two conditions with the word "with", the classification reads it as
"associated with" or "due to" and presumes the relationship without requiring the record to state
it. The presumption holds only for the pairings the index actually lists, and it is overridden when
the documentation says the two are unrelated.

## Unspecified codes, NEC and NOS

**NEC**, not elsewhere classifiable, means the condition is specified but the classification has no
distinct code for it. **NOS**, not otherwise specified, means the documentation was not specific.
The distinction matters because an unspecified code is a statement about the record rather than
about the person, and it remains a valid code: where the documentation genuinely does not support
more detail, the unspecified code is the correct one, and inferring detail the record does not
contain is the error the convention exists to prevent.

[2] (coding-heart-failure-i50)
## The category and its two axes

Heart failure is I50 in ICD-10-CM, at the end of the "other forms of heart disease" block in Chapter
9. Like asthma, it is built from two axes crossed with each other, and unlike asthma both of them
depend entirely on what the record says.

The first axis is mechanism: systolic, diastolic, or combined systolic and diastolic. The second is
acuity: acute, chronic, or acute on chronic, with an unspecified option at each level. The category
also holds left ventricular failure, a set of other specified forms including right heart failure,
biventricular failure, high-output failure and end-stage heart failure, and an unspecified code for
heart failure documented with neither axis.

## The vocabulary problem

Records increasingly describe heart failure by ejection fraction rather than by mechanism — reduced,
preserved, mildly reduced, improved. The classification's terms are the older ones, and the mapping
between the two vocabularies is what most heart-failure coding questions are really about: reduced
ejection fraction corresponds to the systolic branch and preserved ejection fraction to the
diastolic branch. Where the record gives only an ejection fraction number and no descriptive term,
the classification does not permit the mechanism to be derived from it.

"Acute on chronic" requires both to be documented. A chronic condition with a current
decompensation is not automatically coded to that branch unless the record supports both parts.

## Congestive heart failure

"Congestive" is not a fourth branch. The term is inclusive across the category rather than
descriptive of a mechanism, so congestive heart failure with no further detail is coded to the
unspecified code, and congestive heart failure documented as systolic is coded to the systolic
branch. The word does not add specificity even though it reads as though it should.

## Sequencing with hypertensive heart disease

Where the record documents heart disease as hypertensive or as due to hypertension, the combination
code for hypertensive heart disease is reported first and a code from this category is added to
identify the type of heart failure. The hypertension coding note owns which combination code
applies; the point here is that the heart failure code is added rather than replaced.

## What is not coded here

Fluid overload, peripheral edema and pulmonary congestion documented as findings, without a heart
failure diagnosis, are classified with the symptoms and abnormal findings in Chapter 18. Heart
failure following cardiac surgery or a procedure has its own category among the postprocedural
complications. Rheumatic heart failure is classified with the rheumatic block at the start of the
chapter.

## Codes that commonly accompany I50

Chronic kidney disease from the genitourinary chapter and diabetes from the endocrine chapter appear
alongside constantly. Long-term drug therapy, body mass index, and the presence of a cardiac device
are status codes from the factors-influencing-health chapter, and tobacco use or exposure is
requested by categories throughout this chapter.

[3] (coding-icd10-cm-versus-who-icd10)
## Two things share one name

ICD-10 is the World Health Organization's international classification of diseases, used across
countries chiefly for mortality and morbidity statistics. ICD-10-CM is the United States clinical
modification of it, developed and maintained by the National Center for Health Statistics, and it is
what US diagnosis coding actually uses.

The relationship is one of extension rather than translation. The clinical modification keeps the
chapter structure, the letter ranges and most of the three-character categories of the international
version, and then subdivides them much further. A question answered from a WHO ICD-10 reference can
therefore be right about the chapter and wrong about the code.

## What the modification adds

Three additions account for most of the difference in size.

**Laterality.** A large number of categories distinguish right, left, bilateral and unspecified,
which the international version generally does not. This alone multiplies the site-specific
categories in the musculoskeletal and injury chapters.

**Seventh characters.** Injuries, and some obstetric and other categories, carry a character
recording the episode of care rather than anything about the condition — initial encounter,
subsequent encounter, sequela — so one injury generates several valid codes across an episode.

**Greater clinical detail.** Severity, acuteness, laterality and complication status are pushed into
the code itself rather than left to a separate field, and combination codes fold pairs of conditions
together. The diabetes and asthma categories are the clearest examples.

## Procedures are a separate system

The clinical modification covers diagnoses only. Inpatient hospital procedures are coded in
ICD-10-PCS, a structurally unrelated system maintained by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid
Services in which every code is seven characters and each position carries a fixed meaning. Neither
the WHO classification nor the diagnosis modification contains it, and outpatient procedure coding
in the US uses a different system again.

## Updates, and what that means for a stored answer

The clinical modification is revised on an annual cycle, with changes taking effect at the start of
the federal fiscal year on October 1. Categories are added, subdivided and occasionally retired, so
a code that was valid in one year may not be valid in another. Any stored or cached code answer
carries an implicit date, and a lookup against a current file is the only thing that settles
whether a code is still valid.

## Other national modifications, and ICD-11

Several other countries maintain their own clinical modifications of the same international
classification, with their own subdivisions, so "the ICD-10 code" is an underspecified phrase
without a country attached. The World Health Organization has since released ICD-11, which is a
different classification with a different structure rather than a further revision of this one; the
United States has not adopted it for diagnosis coding, and codes do not carry across between them.

[4] (coding-copd-j44)
## The category

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is J44 in ICD-10-CM, in Chapter 10, among the chronic lower
respiratory diseases. Unlike the asthma category beside it, J44 has no severity axis. What its
fourth character records is whether a complication is present at this encounter.

Three subdivisions carry most of the work: the disease with an acute lower respiratory infection,
the disease with an acute exacerbation, and the disease without either, which is the unspecified
code used for a stable presentation. The category also carries subdivisions for other specified
forms.

## The two complication codes are not alternatives

This is the detail that distinguishes J44 from most complication-bearing categories. An infection
and an exacerbation are different events, and someone can have both at once. Where both are
documented, both codes are reported — the classification does not treat the pair as mutually
exclusive the way asthma treats exacerbation and status asthmaticus.

The infection code also does not name the infection. It records that one is present, and a second
code identifying the organism or the specific infection is reported in addition, from whichever
category owns it. Pneumonia accompanying the disease is coded that way rather than being absorbed.

## What the category includes and what sits beside it

The category takes in the overlapping descriptions that clinical records use for the same disease —
chronic obstructive bronchitis, chronic bronchitis with emphysema, chronic obstructive asthma.
Emphysema without chronic bronchitis has its own category, as do simple and mucopurulent chronic
bronchitis and bronchitis not specified as acute or chronic; those are neighbors in the same block,
not subdivisions of this one.

Where asthma is documented alongside, this category carries an instruction to add a code identifying
the type of asthma, so both appear.

## Respiratory failure, and sequencing

Acute or chronic respiratory failure is a separate category at the end of the chapter and is
reported in addition when documented. Which of the two is sequenced first depends on the
circumstances of the encounter rather than on a fixed rule, and it is a sequencing question the
record has to answer.

## Codes that commonly accompany J44

The category carries an explicit instruction to add a code identifying tobacco dependence, use,
exposure or a past history of use, and in practice one of those accompanies most records here.
Occupational or environmental exposure is coded from the factors-influencing-health chapter, with
the external-cause chapter naming the agent. Long-term oxygen use and long-term drug therapy are
status codes. Shortness of breath, cough and sputum production are symptoms intrinsic to the disease
and are not coded separately once it is documented.

[5] (coding-icd10-chapter-03-blood)
## The range and what it holds

Chapter 3 of ICD-10-CM covers D50 through D89: diseases of the blood and blood-forming organs, and
certain disorders involving the immune mechanism. It is the smaller half of the letter D. The first
part of that letter, D00 through D49, belongs to the neoplasm chapter and covers in-situ and benign
tumors, so a D code is not by itself a blood code and the number has to be read before the chapter
is decided.

## The blocks, in order

Nutritional anemias open the chapter at D50 to D53, with iron-deficiency anemia (anaemia) at D50
first, then the deficiencies of vitamin B12 and folate, then other dietary causes. Hemolytic anemias follow across D55 to D59,
divided into the inherited enzyme and hemoglobin disorders and the acquired forms.

Aplastic and other bone-marrow failure anemias occupy D60 to D64, and that block also holds the
residual category for anemias attributed to another disease, which is where anemia of chronic
disease and the anemia accompanying kidney failure are classified.

Coagulation defects, purpura and other hemorrhagic conditions run from D65 to D69, covering the
inherited factor deficiencies, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and the platelet disorders.
Other diseases of the blood and blood-forming organs follow at D70 to D77 — the white-cell
disorders, spleen disorders, and methemoglobinemia among them — with a short block at D78 for
complications of a procedure on the spleen.

The chapter closes at D80 to D89 with certain disorders involving the immune mechanism: the
immunodeficiencies, sarcoidosis, and the residual immune categories.

## What the chapter does not hold, and where those codes live

Cancers of the blood and lymphatic tissue are neoplasms, not blood diseases: leukemia, lymphoma and
myeloma are all classified in Chapter 2, and this chapter's anemia categories are used alongside
them rather than instead of them. Anemia complicating pregnancy, childbirth or the period after
delivery is classified in the obstetric chapter. Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn belongs to the
perinatal chapter.

The boundary that matters most in practice is with abnormal findings. A low hemoglobin (haemoglobin)
or hematocrit on a laboratory report, with no diagnosis of anemia recorded, is an abnormal blood
finding and is classified in Chapter 18, not here. Enlarged lymph nodes with no cause established
are likewise a sign rather than a disease. These codes move into Chapter 3 only when a diagnosis is
documented.

## Codes from other chapters that blood questions commonly need

Anemia is frequently a manifestation rather than a diagnosis in its own right, so the categories
here carry sequencing instructions that reach into other chapters: chronic kidney disease from the
genitourinary chapter, an underlying neoplasm from Chapter 2, and the adverse effect or poisoning
codes from Chapter 19 when a drug is responsible. Chronic blood loss as the cause of iron deficiency
is itself coded from whichever chapter owns the bleeding site. Long-term drug therapy, dietary
counseling encounters and family history all come from the factors-influencing-health chapter.

question: What is described as first-line treatment for newly diagnosed high blood pressure?
answer:
According to current guidelines from a major cardiology society, the first-line treatment for newly diagnosed high blood pressure typically involves drug treatment in conjunction with lifestyle measures. The recommendations are as follows:

1. **For Stage 1 hypertension with certain conditions**: If a person has established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or a 10-year cardiovascular risk of 10% or more, drug treatment should be started along with lifestyle measures.

2. **For Stage 1 hypertension without those features**: Lifestyle measures should be implemented first, with a reassessment in three to six months to determine if drug treatment is necessary.

The first-line drug classes for hypertension are:
- Thiazide-type diuretics
- Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors
- Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs)
- Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers

It is important to note that ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used together, as this combination can lead to harm without added benefit. This guidance comes from the document titled "Hypertension: when treatment starts and which options are first-line" (Major cardiology society consensus guidance).

[1] (guideline-hypertension-first-line-treatment)
## Lifestyle measures are the shared foundation

Every major body recommends the same set of non-drug measures, whether or not medication is also
used: reducing dietary sodium, adopting a dietary pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains
and low-fat dairy and low in saturated fat, regular aerobic activity most days of the week, weight
reduction where body weight is above the healthy range, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking.
Each produces a meaningful reduction on its own, and the effects are partly additive, so several
combined can move a person a full stage.

## When drug treatment starts

The decision is tied to cardiovascular risk, not to the blood-pressure number alone:

- **Stage 2 hypertension** — drug treatment alongside lifestyle measures, usually beginning with
  two agents, because a single agent rarely closes a gap of this size.
- **Stage 1 hypertension with established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney
  disease, or an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk at or above 10 percent** — drug treatment
  alongside lifestyle measures.
- **Stage 1 hypertension without those features** — lifestyle measures first, with reassessment
  after three to six months before drug treatment is considered.

## First-line drug classes

Four classes are first-line for most adults without a compelling indication for something else:
thiazide-type diuretics, angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers,
and dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers. An ACE inhibitor and an angiotensin receptor blocker
are not combined — the combination adds harm without adding benefit. Single-pill combinations are
preferred where two agents are needed, because adherence falls as pill count rises.

Comorbidity shifts the choice. Renin-angiotensin blockade is preferred where diabetes with
albuminuria or chronic kidney disease is present; a beta-blocker is not first-line for uncomplicated
hypertension but becomes appropriate where there is a separate indication such as heart failure or
recent myocardial infarction. Doses are outside the scope of this note and of this system.

## Resistant hypertension

Blood pressure above target on three agents including a diuretic, all at appropriate doses, is
described as resistant hypertension. Before treatment is escalated further, the sequence is to
confirm the readings out of office, review adherence, review agents that raise blood pressure —
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, decongestants, some stimulants, combined oral contraceptives
— and investigate for a secondary cause. Apparent resistance is more often measurement, adherence
or an interfering agent than a need for a fourth drug.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on how aggressively to treat low-risk stage 1 hypertension, which follows from the
threshold disagreement in the diagnostic note: where guidance describes hypertension as beginning at
140/90 mm Hg, much of the population that United States guidance calls stage 1 is instead advised on
lifestyle alone.

## Follow-up interval

Monthly review until the target is reached, including adherence and a check of kidney function and
potassium after starting an agent acting on the renin-angiotensin system, then review every three
to six months once stable.

[2] (guideline-anxiety-screening-and-first-line-care)
## Screening

Preventive-services guidance describes screening adults for anxiety disorders where systems are in
place to ensure accurate diagnosis and follow-up, with the strongest statement made for adults under
65. For older adults the evidence is judged insufficient to make a recommendation either way — a
statement about the evidence, not a recommendation against screening, and one that is frequently
misread as the latter.

The seven-item generalized anxiety disorder questionnaire (generalised in British spelling) is the
instrument most often used, both to screen and to track severity. The commonly used severity bands
are 5 for mild, 10 for moderate and 15 for severe, with 10 the threshold at which further assessment
usually follows. A questionnaire score is not a diagnosis: it prompts a diagnostic assessment, which
includes ruling out physical causes such as thyroid disease and arrhythmia, reviewing substance,
caffeine and medication effects, and assessing for co-occurring depression, which is common enough
that finding one is a reason to look for the other.

## First-line treatment

Two first-line options of broadly comparable effectiveness, chosen with the person rather than for
them:

- **Cognitive behavioral therapy**, delivered individually, in a group, or through a guided digital
  program, with the largest evidence base of the psychological therapies.
- **Pharmacotherapy** with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor or a serotonin-noradrenaline
  reuptake inhibitor.

Combining the two is usual for more severe or non-responding presentations. Availability, waiting
times and preference legitimately drive the choice, since a treatment that starts is better than a
better treatment that does not.

## Timing of review

Response is reviewed at four to six weeks after medication starts, with the caveat that anxiety
symptoms can transiently worsen in the first days — a predictable effect worth warning about in
advance, because it is a common reason for stopping early. Eight to twelve weeks at an adequate dose
precedes any conclusion that an agent has failed. Where a first agent fails, switching within or
between classes comes before adding further agents.

## Duration and stopping

Where treatment is effective, it continues for six to twelve months before a gradual taper is
considered, because early discontinuation is associated with relapse. Tapering is gradual and
monitored rather than abrupt, and discontinuation symptoms are distinguished from a return of the
underlying disorder, which they closely resemble and which they precede in time.

## Benzodiazepines

Benzodiazepines are not first-line for generalized anxiety disorder and are inappropriate for
long-term use: tolerance, dependence, cognitive effects, falls in older adults, and no effect on the
underlying disorder. Where used at all, the role is short and bounded.

## What is outside this note

Doses and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this system. Thoughts of
self-harm or suicide are an urgent situation covered by the emergency guidance elsewhere in this
corpus, not by routine review.

[3] (guideline-type-2-diabetes-first-line-therapy)
## The shape of current guidance

Older guidance set out a single sequence: metformin first, then agents added in order as control
worsened. Current guidance is structured differently — the first-line choice depends on which other
conditions are present, and for several of them the choice is made independently of the HbA1c value.
This is the substantive change, and it is the part most often stated in the old form.

## Where there is no compelling comorbidity

Metformin, alongside structured lifestyle intervention, is the usual initial agent: long experience,
low cost, weight neutrality, and little risk of causing low blood sugar on its own. Kidney function
is checked before starting and periodically after, since the dose is constrained below a threshold
of kidney function and the agent is avoided below a lower one. Gastrointestinal intolerance is the
common reason for stopping, and is reduced by gradual escalation and extended-release formulations.
Long-term use is associated with lower vitamin B12 levels, so periodic measurement is advised.

## Where cardiovascular, kidney or heart-failure disease is present

Guidance describes agents with demonstrated organ benefit as preferred, whether or not metformin is
also used, and independent of whether the HbA1c is at goal:

- **Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease** — a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven
  cardiovascular benefit, or an SGLT-2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit.
- **Heart failure**, particularly with reduced ejection fraction — an SGLT-2 inhibitor.
- **Chronic kidney disease**, particularly with albuminuria — an SGLT-2 inhibitor, with a GLP-1
  receptor agonist as the alternative where an SGLT-2 inhibitor is not tolerated or not appropriate.

These are organ-protective therapies that also lower glucose, rather than later steps in a glucose
ladder. Class-specific cautions are part of the choice: SGLT-2 inhibitors carry a risk of genital
mycotic infection, volume depletion, and — uncommonly — ketoacidosis at near-normal glucose levels,
which is easy to miss precisely because the glucose is not high.

## Where weight is a major treatment goal

Agents with the greatest weight-reduction effect — the GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual incretin
agonists — are preferred where weight management is a primary objective, alongside structured
lifestyle intervention and, in selected people, metabolic surgery.

## Reassessment

The regimen is reviewed every three to six months. De-intensification is an explicit option, not a
failure: where the regimen has become more aggressive than the individualized target requires, or
where low blood sugar is occurring, stepping down is the appropriate response.

Doses, titration schedules and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this
system.

[4] (guideline-hypertension-diagnosis-and-bp-targets)
## What this guidance covers

How adult office blood pressure is classified, what is required before a diagnosis of hypertension
is made, and the treatment target most bodies set once treatment has begun.

## Classification of office blood pressure in adults

United States society guidance classifies adult office readings as:

- **Normal** — systolic below 120 mm Hg *and* diastolic below 80 mm Hg.
- **Elevated** — systolic 120 to 129 mm Hg *and* diastolic below 80 mm Hg.
- **Stage 1 hypertension** — systolic 130 to 139 mm Hg *or* diastolic 80 to 89 mm Hg.
- **Stage 2 hypertension** — systolic at least 140 mm Hg *or* diastolic at least 90 mm Hg.

When the systolic and diastolic values fall into different categories, the higher category applies.
"Elevated" is not a stage of hypertension: it marks a group at raised future risk in whom lifestyle
measures are advised and drug treatment is not.

## Measurement technique, which changes the number

A reading taken carelessly is not a milder version of a correct reading — it is a different
measurement. The technique that the classification above assumes is a validated device, a cuff
sized to the arm, the person seated with back supported and feet flat, arm supported at heart
level, no caffeine, exercise or smoking in the preceding 30 minutes, five minutes of rest
beforehand, and no talking during the measurement. An undersized cuff and an unsupported arm both
push the reading up, each by an amount comparable to the width of a whole stage.

## Confirming the diagnosis

A diagnosis is not made from a single reading. The standard is an average of two or more readings
taken on two or more separate occasions. Out-of-office measurement — home readings or 24-hour
ambulatory monitoring — confirms the diagnosis and identifies two patterns that office readings
alone cannot: white-coat hypertension, where office readings are raised but out-of-office readings
are not, and masked hypertension, where the reverse holds and the risk is underestimated.

## Treatment target

For most treated adults, United States guidance describes a target below 130/80 mm Hg. The target is
individualized for older adults with frailty, limited life expectancy, or a heavy burden of other
conditions, where the balance of benefit and harm differs and where postural drops matter more.

## Where guidance differs

The 130/80 mm Hg diagnostic threshold is a United States position. European guidance describes office
hypertension as beginning at 140/90 mm Hg, and treats the 130 to 139 / 80 to 89 band as high-normal
blood pressure rather than as stage 1 disease. The same reading is therefore labeled differently
depending on which body's guidance is applied, and the size of the population called hypertensive
changes substantially between the two. Any answer that quotes a threshold should say which
convention it is using.

## Follow-up interval

After treatment starts or changes, reassessment at roughly monthly intervals until the target is
reached, then review every three to six months once readings are stable.

[5] (guideline-coronary-artery-disease-secondary-prevention)
## What secondary prevention means

Secondary prevention is the set of measures used for someone who already has established coronary
artery disease — a previous heart attack, a revascularization procedure, or angiographic disease —
to reduce the chance of a further event. It is a package rather than a single intervention: no one
element carries the effect, and the benefit measured in trials comes from applying them together.
Partial application is the common failure, and it is usually the non-drug elements that are dropped.

## The components

- **Antiplatelet therapy** — long-term single antiplatelet therapy for most people, with a defined
  period of dual antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome or stent placement, its
  duration individualized against bleeding risk.
- **High-intensity statin therapy**. United States guidance describes the intensity; European
  guidance describes an LDL goal instead. Where the response is inadequate, additional
  non-statin agents are added rather than the statin abandoned.
- **Blood-pressure control**, with a target below 130/80 mm Hg for most people.
- **Renin-angiotensin blockade** where diabetes, reduced left ventricular function, or chronic
  kidney disease is also present.
- **Beta-blockade** after myocardial infarction, with the strongest and longest-standing evidence
  where left ventricular function is reduced.
- **Cardiac rehabilitation referral** — a structured program of supervised exercise, education and
  risk-factor management, and consistently one of the most underused elements relative to the
  strength of the evidence behind it.
- **Smoking cessation**, the single largest modifiable factor, with combined behavioral and
  pharmacologic support more effective than advice alone.
- **Annual influenza vaccination**, included as a cardiovascular measure rather than only a
  respiratory one.
- **Structured management of diabetes** where present, preferring agents with demonstrated
  cardiovascular benefit.

## Review interval

Review at least annually once the regimen is stable, with earlier review after any change in
symptoms, after a hospital admission, and four to twelve weeks after any change in lipid-lowering
intensity. Each review is an opportunity to check adherence, which falls measurably in the year
after an event as the acute experience recedes.

## What warrants urgent reassessment

New, worsening, or rest-onset chest discomfort in someone with known coronary disease is not a
routine review matter and requires urgent assessment. A pattern of angina that is becoming more
frequent, more easily provoked, or longer-lasting is a change in category rather than a change in
degree. The emergency-symptom notes elsewhere in this corpus govern these situations, and this note
does not substitute for them.

question: When does guidance describe antivirals as worth considering for influenza?
answer:
The guidance on antiviral treatment for influenza highlights several important considerations regarding their use:

1. **Timing of Treatment**: Antiviral treatment is most effective when started within 48 hours of the onset of symptoms. If initiated within this time frame, there is a significant benefit in symptom reduction. The effectiveness lessens as the window for starting treatment closes.

2. **Indications for Treatment**:
   - **Hospitalized Patients**: Antivirals are strongly recommended for anyone hospitalized with suspected or confirmed influenza.
   - **Severe Cases**: Individuals with severe, complicated, or progressive illness should receive antiviral treatment as soon as possible, even before laboratory confirmation.
   - **High-Risk Patients**: Those who are at higher risk for complications from influenza should also be treated promptly.

3. **Outpatients**: For otherwise healthy outpatients who present with symptoms within 48 hours, antiviral treatment is considered a reasonable option. This is based on shared decision-making, as it leads to a modest reduction in the duration of symptoms.

4. **Delayed Treatment**: Treatment initiated after 48 hours can still be appropriate for hospitalized and severely ill patients, as some observational evidence suggests potential benefit even beyond the initial 48-hour window.

This guidance comes from the "Influenza: annual vaccination and the timing of antiviral treatment" document by the National Immunization Advisory Committee and Infectious Diseases Society (educational summary).

## Annual vaccination

United States guidance describes routine annual influenza vaccination for everyone aged 6 months and
older who has no contraindication, rather than restricting it to high-risk groups. Vaccination
before the end of October is described as the usual aim in the northern hemisphere, early enough to
precede typical circulation and not so early that protection wanes before the season ends. Later
vaccination remains worthwhile while the virus is circulating.

Annual repetition is necessary for two reasons that are often conflated: the circulating strains
change, so the vaccine composition is reformulated each year, and protection from a given dose wanes
over months regardless.

Higher-dose or adjuvanted formulations are preferentially described for adults aged 65 and over, in
whom the standard-dose response is weaker. Egg-free formulations exist, and current guidance
describes egg allergy of any severity as no longer requiring special precautions beyond those for
any vaccine.

Adults 65 and over, children under 5 and especially under 2, pregnancy and the postpartum period,
residents of long-term care, people with chronic lung, heart, kidney, liver, neurologic or metabolic
disease, immunosuppression, and people with a body mass index in the obese range. Vaccination in
pregnancy also confers protection on the infant in the first months of life, before the infant can
be vaccinated directly. Health-care workers are included on transmission grounds as well as personal
ones.

Antiviral treatment is described as most effective when started within 48 hours of symptom onset,
and the benefit falls as that window closes. Treatment is recommended as early as possible, without
waiting for laboratory confirmation, for:

- Anyone hospitalized with suspected or confirmed influenza.
- Anyone with severe, complicated or progressive illness.
- Anyone at higher risk of complications, per the groups above.

For otherwise healthy outpatients presenting within 48 hours, treatment is described as a
reasonable option based on shared decision-making, with a modest reduction in symptom duration.
Treatment started after 48 hours is still described as appropriate in hospitalized and severely ill
patients, where observational evidence supports benefit beyond the outpatient window.

Antibiotics have no activity against influenza and are reserved for bacterial complications.

Bodies differ on antiviral use in low-risk outpatients. Some guidance describes it as a reasonable
option for symptom reduction; other guidance and independent evidence reviews are more restrictive,
holding that the effect on symptom duration is modest, the effect on complications and
hospitalization in this group is not well established, and routine use is not justified. Answers
should distinguish the high-risk recommendation, which is consistent, from the low-risk one, which
is not.

## The diagnosis is spirometric

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is not diagnosed from symptoms alone. A post-bronchodilator
ratio of forced expiratory volume in one second to forced vital capacity below 0.70 confirms
persistent airflow limitation, in a person with compatible symptoms — breathlessness on exertion,
chronic cough, sputum production — and a relevant exposure history, most often tobacco smoke, and
also biomass fuel and occupational dust or fumes. The degree of airflow limitation is graded
separately, using the forced expiratory volume as a percentage of predicted, and correlates only
loosely with how the person actually feels.

Two axes are assessed rather than severity alone. Symptom burden is measured with a standard
questionnaire or breathlessness scale, and exacerbation history over the past year is recorded, with
particular weight on any exacerbation requiring hospital admission. Together they place the person
in a group that determines initial therapy. The exacerbation axis, not the symptom axis, identifies
the group at highest risk — and the best predictor of a future exacerbation is a past one.

Guidance describes initial therapy by group rather than by severity of airflow limitation:

- **Low symptom burden, no significant exacerbation history** — a long-acting bronchodilator.
- **High symptom burden, no significant exacerbation history** — dual long-acting bronchodilator
  therapy, combining a muscarinic antagonist and a beta-agonist.
- **Significant exacerbation history** — dual long-acting bronchodilator therapy, with an inhaled
  corticosteroid added where the blood eosinophil count is high or where features of coexisting
  asthma are present.

corticosteroid. The decision rests on a marker rather than being applied to everyone because
inhaled corticosteroid use in this population carries an increased risk of pneumonia, so the benefit
has to be identifiable to be worth the harm.

common avoidable errors in the pathway.

## What secondary prevention means

Secondary prevention is the set of measures used for someone who already has established coronary
artery disease — a previous heart attack, a revascularization procedure, or angiographic disease —
to reduce the chance of a further event. It is a package rather than a single intervention: no one
element carries the effect, and the benefit measured in trials comes from applying them together.
Partial application is the common failure, and it is usually the non-drug elements that are dropped.

## The components

- **Antiplatelet therapy** — long-term single antiplatelet therapy for most people, with a defined
  period of dual antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome or stent placement, its
  duration individualized against bleeding risk.
- **High-intensity statin therapy**. United States guidance describes the intensity; European
  guidance describes an LDL goal instead. Where the response is inadequate, additional
  non-statin agents are added rather than the statin abandoned.
- **Blood-pressure control**, with a target below 130/80 mm Hg for most people.
- **Renin-angiotensin blockade** where diabetes, reduced left ventricular function, or chronic
  kidney disease is also present.
- **Beta-blockade** after myocardial infarction, with the strongest and longest-standing evidence
  where left ventricular function is reduced.
- **Cardiac rehabilitation referral** — a structured program of supervised exercise, education and
  risk-factor management, and consistently one of the most underused elements relative to the
  strength of the evidence behind it.
- **Smoking cessation**, the single largest modifiable factor, with combined behavioral and
  pharmacologic support more effective than advice alone.
- **Annual influenza vaccination**, included as a cardiovascular measure rather than only a
  respiratory one.
- **Structured management of diabetes** where present, preferring agents with demonstrated
  cardiovascular benefit.

Review at least annually once the regimen is stable, with earlier review after any change in
symptoms, after a hospital admission, and four to twelve weeks after any change in lipid-lowering
intensity. Each review is an opportunity to check adherence, which falls measurably in the year
after an event as the acute experience recedes.

routine review matter and requires urgent assessment. A pattern of angina that is becoming more
frequent, more easily provoked, or longer-lasting is a change in category rather than a change in
degree. The emergency-symptom notes elsewhere in this corpus govern these situations, and this note
does not substitute for them.

## Acute treatment

An attack is treated early, while pain is still mild, because response rates fall once an attack is
established and central sensitization has set in. The options are grouped by evidence strength
rather than presented as a ranked list for an individual:

- Simple analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for mild to moderate attacks.
- Triptans for moderate to severe attacks, or where simple analgesics have failed.
- The gepant and ditan classes where triptans are ineffective, not tolerated, or contraindicated by
  cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease — which is the main limitation on triptan use.
- Anti-nausea agents as adjuncts where nausea limits oral treatment; non-oral routes where vomiting
  or gastric stasis makes an oral route unreliable.

Treating on two or three separate attacks before judging an agent ineffective is the usual standard,
since attack-to-attack variability is high.

## When preventive treatment starts

Preventive treatment is offered when attacks are frequent or disabling enough that acute treatment
alone is insufficient. Guidance describes the threshold as four or more migraine days per month with
some disability, or fewer attacks where disability is severe, where acute treatment is ineffective
or contraindicated, or where the person prefers it. The aim is a reduction in frequency and
severity, not the elimination of attacks: a 50 percent reduction in migraine days is the conventional
definition of a treatment response.

## Preventive classes

Classes with supporting evidence include beta-blockers, the antiepileptics topiramate and valproate,
the tricyclic amitriptyline, candesartan, and the CGRP-targeted monoclonal antibodies and oral
gepants. The choice is made on comorbidity, side-effect profile and pregnancy status rather than by
a fixed order — an agent that also treats a coexisting condition is preferred, and valproate and
topiramate require particular care in people who could become pregnant.

## Assessing response

An adequate trial precedes any judgment of failure: commonly eight to twelve weeks at an appropriate
dose. A headache diary is the instrument for that judgment, because recall of attack frequency is
unreliable and tends to be dominated by the worst recent attack rather than the average.

## Medication-overuse headache

This is the point guidance emphasizes most. Frequent use of acute medication can itself sustain a
headache disorder, converting an episodic pattern into a chronic one. The limits are fewer than ten
treatment days per month for triptans, ergots, opioids and combination analgesics, and fewer than
fifteen days per month for simple analgesics. Overuse is a common and reversible reason for
headaches having become chronic, and it is checked for before a preventive regimen is escalated.

## What is outside this note

Doses, titration and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this system.
Sudden severe headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute, headache with fever and neck
stiffness, headache with new neurological deficit, and headache after head injury are emergency
presentations covered elsewhere in this corpus, not migraine management questions.

## What counts as chronic insomnia

Chronic insomnia disorder is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking too early,
occurring at least three nights per week for at least three months, despite adequate opportunity to
sleep, and accompanied by daytime consequences — fatigue, impaired attention, mood disturbance, or
impaired performance. The daytime component is part of the definition: short sleep without daytime
consequences is not a disorder, and treating it as one medicalizes normal variation in sleep need.

Assessment includes a sleep diary over one to two weeks, screening for the conditions that commonly
present as insomnia — obstructive sleep apnea (apnoea), restless legs syndrome, circadian rhythm
disorders, depression, anxiety, pain, and substance or medication effects — and review of caffeine,
alcohol, nicotine and shift patterns. Alcohol is worth singling out: it shortens sleep latency and
then fragments the second half of the night, so it is often reported as a remedy by someone whose
sleep it is degrading.

## The first-line recommendation

Both sleep medicine and internal medicine guidance describes cognitive behavioral therapy for
insomnia as first-line for chronic insomnia in adults, ahead of medication. Its effects persist after treatment
ends, whereas pharmacological effects generally do not, and it avoids the harms associated with
long-term hypnotic use.

The components are delivered together as a package over roughly four to eight sessions:

- **Stimulus control** — using the bed only for sleep, leaving the bed when unable to sleep, so the
  bed stops being a cue for wakefulness.
- **Sleep restriction** — limiting time in bed toward actual sleep time, then extending it as sleep
  consolidates. Counterintuitive, and the component people most often abandon early.
- **Cognitive restructuring** of the beliefs about sleep that maintain arousal, including the
  catastrophizing about tomorrow that keeps someone awake tonight.
- **Sleep hygiene education**, necessary but insufficient on its own. Guidance is explicit that
  sleep hygiene advice alone is not effective treatment for chronic insomnia — a frequent
  misunderstanding, and the reason that "I already tried sleep hygiene" is not evidence that this
  therapy has been tried.
- **Relaxation training.**

Digitally delivered and brief formats are reasonable where in-person therapy is not accessible,
which is the practical constraint most often cited against the recommendation.

## Where medication sits

Pharmacotherapy is second-line: for people in whom cognitive behavioral therapy is unavailable, has
been tried without adequate response, or where short-term treatment is needed alongside it. Shared
decision-making, the shortest appropriate duration, and a plan for reassessment and discontinuation
agreed at the point of starting rather than later. Antihistamine-based over-the-counter sleep aids
have limited evidence and notable anticholinergic side effects, particularly in older adults.

## What is outside this note

Doses and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this system.

question: What does asthma guidance describe as the stepwise approach, and what changed about reliever choice?
answer:
The stepwise approach in asthma management involves adjusting treatment based on the patient's current symptom control and exacerbation history. It is organized into different steps, each offering progressively stronger medication options. Reviews of the patient's condition are essential and should take place one to three months after starting or changing therapy, then every three to twelve months thereafter (Global respiratory strategy report and national asthma panel guidance).

A significant update is that using a short-acting bronchodilator alone is no longer recommended for any severity of asthma. Patients are now prescribed inhaled corticosteroids even for those with infrequent symptoms, as relying solely on reliever medication does not address underlying inflammation and can lead to severe exacerbations (Global respiratory strategy report and national asthma panel guidance).

Regarding reliever choices, there is disagreement in the guidance. The global strategy recommends using a combination of inhaled corticosteroid and formoterol as the preferred reliever at all steps of asthma management. In contrast, some national guidelines still suggest that a short-acting bronchodilator is appropriate for patients with mild asthma alongside their regular controller (Global respiratory strategy report and national asthma panel guidance).

## Confirming the diagnosis

Asthma requires both a compatible symptom pattern and objective evidence of variable expiratory
airflow limitation. The symptom pattern is variable wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and
cough, worse at night or early morning and provoked by exercise, allergens, cold air or viral
infection. The objective test is spirometry before and after a bronchodilator, with reversibility
supporting the diagnosis.

A normal spirometry result when the person is well does not exclude asthma — variability is the
point, and a measurement taken on a good day measures the good day. Repeat testing while
symptomatic, peak-flow variability over two weeks, or bronchial challenge testing are the usual next
steps where the diagnosis remains uncertain. Confirming it before committing someone to long-term
inhaled therapy matters, because a substantial share of people carrying an asthma label do not have
objective confirmation of it.

## The central change in modern guidance

Treating asthma with a short-acting bronchodilator alone is no longer appropriate at any severity.
Every adult and adolescent with asthma receives inhaled-corticosteroid-containing therapy, because
reliever-only treatment leaves the underlying inflammation untreated and is associated with severe
exacerbations even in people whose symptoms are infrequent. Heavy reliever use — several canisters a
year — is a marker of risk in its own right.

## The stepwise structure

Treatment is arranged in steps, with the step chosen from current symptom control and exacerbation
history and reviewed rather than fixed:

- **Lower steps** — as-needed inhaled corticosteroid combined with a fast-onset long-acting
  bronchodilator, or regular low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with an as-needed reliever.
- **Middle steps** — regular low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting bronchodilator, with
  the same combination inhaler used as the reliever in one of the described regimens.
- **Higher steps** — medium- or high-dose combination therapy, the addition of a long-acting
  muscarinic antagonist, then referral for severe-asthma assessment including biologic agents
  targeted to inflammatory phenotype.

Stepping down is considered after three or more months of good control. Before stepping up, inhaler
technique and adherence are checked, since between them they account for a large share of apparent
treatment failure, and a step-up that compensates for poor technique treats the wrong problem.

## Where guidance differs

The preferred reliever in mild asthma is a genuine point of divergence. Global strategy guidance
describes an inhaled-corticosteroid-and-formoterol combination as the preferred reliever across
steps; some national panel guidance describes a short-acting bronchodilator reliever alongside a
regular controller as remaining appropriate in mild disease. Answers should name which position they are describing.

## Review interval

Review one to three months after starting or changing therapy, then every three to twelve months,
and within one week after an exacerbation — the period when the reason for the exacerbation is still
recoverable.

## The core recommendation

Every major body places non-pharmacologic management first, and this is not a courtesy placement
ahead of the real treatment. Structured exercise carries the strongest and most consistent evidence
of any intervention for knee and hip osteoarthritis, with effect sizes comparable to pharmacologic
options and a far better harm profile.

The described program combines muscle strengthening around the affected joint, range-of-movement
work, and aerobic activity, delivered with supervision at least initially, because adherence and
correct progression determine the result. Exercise is described as beneficial regardless of
radiographic severity, age, or degree of pain at the outset — the common belief that a badly worn
joint should be rested is contradicted by the evidence, and pain during exercise within tolerable
limits is not a sign of damage.

Weight management is described alongside it where body weight is above the healthy range, with
clinically meaningful improvement at reductions of five to ten percent and further gains beyond
that. The two together outperform either alone.

## Adjunctive non-drug measures

Education and self-management support, pacing, appropriate footwear, walking aids where they
improve function, and heat or cold for symptomatic relief. Braces and orthoses are described for
selected patterns. Acupuncture, ultrasound, and similar modalities are described with weak or
conflicting evidence, and guidance differs on whether to mention them at all.

## Pharmacologic options

Described as adjuncts to the exercise program rather than as substitutes for it:

- **Topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs** — preferred first pharmacologic option for knee
  and hand osteoarthritis, with lower systemic exposure than oral agents.
- **Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs** — effective, at the lowest effective dose for the
  shortest period, with gastrointestinal, cardiovascular and kidney risk assessed first.
- **Intra-articular corticosteroid injection** — short-term relief for a flare, with the effect
  measured in weeks.
- **Duloxetine** — described for people with widespread pain or inadequate response to the above.

Opioids are described as not recommended for osteoarthritis, on evidence of limited benefit and
substantial harm. Glucosamine and chondroitin are described as not recommended by most bodies, on
evidence of no clinically meaningful effect. Doses are outside the scope of this system.

## Surgery

Joint replacement is described for people with persistent pain and functional limitation despite
adequate non-surgical management, and it is highly effective in that group. Arthroscopic surgery for
degenerative knee disease is described as not recommended, on evidence showing no benefit over
placebo procedures.

Intra-articular corticosteroid injection is a live disagreement. Some guidance describes it as a
conditional recommendation for short-term relief; other guidance is more cautious, citing modest
duration of benefit and evidence suggesting repeated injections may be associated with cartilage
loss. Bodies also differ on topical capsaicin and on whether platelet-rich plasma and similar
injectables should be mentioned as options or explicitly discouraged.

## The default position

Acute upper respiratory infections — the common cold, most sore throats, acute bronchitis, and
uncomplicated acute sinusitis in its first days — are viral in the large majority of cases, and
antibiotics do not shorten them, do not prevent complications at a rate that justifies routine use,
and do cause harm: adverse effects, allergic reactions, disruption of normal flora, *Clostridioides
difficile* infection, and selection for resistant organisms in the individual as well as the
population.

Guidance describes not prescribing antibiotics for these presentations as the active recommendation,
not merely the absence of one. Communication is treated as part of the clinical intervention:
explaining the expected course, naming the duration, describing what would change the plan, and
offering symptomatic measures reduces both prescribing and dissatisfaction, whereas a bare refusal
does neither.

## What does not indicate a bacterial infection

- **Discolored nasal discharge.** Yellow or green discharge is part of the normal viral course.
- **Duration alone within the expected window.** A cold lasting seven to ten days is running its
  course; cough alone persisting two to three weeks after a cold is expected.
- **Low-grade fever** in the first days.
- **Productive cough** in acute bronchitis, which is viral in the overwhelming majority of
  otherwise healthy adults.

## When antibiotics are described as indicated

- **Acute bacterial sinusitis**, identified by one of three patterns rather than by symptoms alone:
  symptoms persisting ten days or more without improvement; severe symptoms with high fever and
  purulent discharge for three to four consecutive days at onset; or the "double worsening" pattern
  in which symptoms improve and then deteriorate.
- **Group A streptococcal pharyngitis**, confirmed by rapid antigen testing or culture rather than
  by appearance. Clinical scoring systems select who to test; they do not replace the test, since
  the features overlap heavily with viral pharyngitis.
- **Pneumonia**, suspected on focal findings, abnormal vital signs, or a compatible chest image —
  a different diagnosis rather than an upper respiratory infection that has gone on too long.
- **Complications** such as peritonsillar abscess, or infection in someone significantly
  immunocompromised.

## Delayed prescribing

A prescription given with instructions to fill it only if symptoms fail to improve or worsen by a
stated point is described as a middle option, reducing antibiotic use substantially compared with
immediate prescribing while maintaining satisfaction. It is described as most useful where the
clinician judges bacterial infection unlikely but the person's expectation or access to follow-up
argues against a plain refusal.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on how far the delayed-prescription strategy should be encouraged. Some describe it as
a recommended tool for reducing immediate prescribing; others are wary, on the grounds that it still
results in a prescription in a substantial fraction of cases and may reinforce the expectation that
these illnesses warrant antibiotics at all. Guidance also differs on sore-throat management, with
some national guidance placing greater weight on clinical scoring and less on universal testing
before treatment.

## Lifestyle measures are the shared foundation

Every major body recommends the same set of non-drug measures, whether or not medication is also
used: reducing dietary sodium, adopting a dietary pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains
and low-fat dairy and low in saturated fat, regular aerobic activity most days of the week, weight
reduction where body weight is above the healthy range, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking.
Each produces a meaningful reduction on its own, and the effects are partly additive, so several
combined can move a person a full stage.

## When drug treatment starts

The decision is tied to cardiovascular risk, not to the blood-pressure number alone:

- **Stage 2 hypertension** — drug treatment alongside lifestyle measures, usually beginning with
  two agents, because a single agent rarely closes a gap of this size.
- **Stage 1 hypertension with established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney
  disease, or an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk at or above 10 percent** — drug treatment
  alongside lifestyle measures.
- **Stage 1 hypertension without those features** — lifestyle measures first, with reassessment
  after three to six months before drug treatment is considered.

## First-line drug classes

Four classes are first-line for most adults without a compelling indication for something else:
thiazide-type diuretics, angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers,
and dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers. An ACE inhibitor and an angiotensin receptor blocker
are not combined — the combination adds harm without adding benefit. Single-pill combinations are
preferred where two agents are needed, because adherence falls as pill count rises.

Comorbidity shifts the choice. Renin-angiotensin blockade is preferred where diabetes with
albuminuria or chronic kidney disease is present; a beta-blocker is not first-line for uncomplicated
hypertension but becomes appropriate where there is a separate indication such as heart failure or
recent myocardial infarction. Doses are outside the scope of this note and of this system.

## Resistant hypertension

Blood pressure above target on three agents including a diuretic, all at appropriate doses, is
described as resistant hypertension. Before treatment is escalated further, the sequence is to
confirm the readings out of office, review adherence, review agents that raise blood pressure —
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, decongestants, some stimulants, combined oral contraceptives
— and investigate for a secondary cause. Apparent resistance is more often measurement, adherence
or an interfering agent than a need for a fourth drug.

question: What TSH range does guidance describe as the treatment threshold in subclinical hypothyroidism?
answer:
Guidance on the treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism shows some variability. Generally, there is broad agreement that treatment should start when thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels are persistently above about 10 mIU/L. However, there is a "band" between the upper reference limit (often around 4.5-5.0 mIU/L) and 10 mIU/L where opinions diverge.

In this intermediate range, some guidelines advocate for considering treatment if symptoms, positive thyroid antibodies, or cardiovascular risk factors are present. Other guidelines recommend monitoring without immediate treatment, based on evidence suggesting no significant symptomatic benefit from treating older adults with TSH levels in this range.

This information comes from the "Endocrinology and thyroid association guidance" which highlights the areas where guidance differs regarding treatment for subclinical hypothyroidism.
