[1] (condition-insomnia)
## What it is

Insomnia is difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking earlier than intended, despite
adequate opportunity to sleep, together with daytime consequences. Both halves are required. Sleeping
six hours and functioning well is not insomnia; sleeping six hours and being impaired by it may be.
The condition is defined by the mismatch between sleep obtained and sleep needed, not by a clock
value.

Short-term insomnia lasting days to weeks, usually with an identifiable precipitant, is common and
often self-limiting. Chronic insomnia disorder — at least three nights per week for at least three
months — is a distinct condition that persists after the original precipitant has resolved.

## Why it persists after the trigger goes

This is the part that explains the treatment. An episode is typically precipitated by stress,
illness or a schedule change. What perpetuates it are the responses: going to bed earlier to
"catch up", staying in bed awake, daytime napping, and increasing effort to fall asleep. Time in bed
rises while sleep does not, so the bed becomes associated with wakefulness, and the effort itself
increases arousal. The condition then maintains itself independently of what started it — which is
why treatment targets those perpetuating behaviors rather than the original stressor.

## How it is usually recognized

The account of the sleep pattern, supported by a sleep diary kept over one to two weeks. Diaries
matter because recall systematically overestimates how long it took to fall asleep and underestimates
total sleep — the periods of sleep between awakenings are not remembered.

## What else presents as insomnia

Obstructive sleep apnea (apnoea), restless legs syndrome, circadian rhythm disorders including shift
work and delayed sleep phase, chronic pain, depression, anxiety, and the effects of caffeine,
alcohol, nicotine, stimulants and some prescribed medications. Screening for these is part of the
assessment rather than a step taken only when treatment fails, because treating the wrong condition
is the most common reason for non-response. Alcohol deserves specific mention: it shortens the time
to fall asleep and fragments the second half of the night, so it is frequently reported as a remedy
by someone whose sleep it is degrading.

## Why it is treated

Chronic insomnia is associated with impaired daytime function, reduced quality of life, and
increased risk of depression, and it complicates the management of coexisting physical illness. It
also responds durably to non-drug treatment, which makes long-term reliance on hypnotics avoidable
for most people.

## How it is generally managed

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia is first-line, with medication second-line and
time-limited. The components, the evidence, and the specific point that sleep hygiene advice alone
is not effective treatment are covered by the insomnia guideline note in this corpus.

## When further assessment is advised

Loud snoring with witnessed pauses in breathing, excessive daytime sleepiness, falling asleep while
driving, acting out dreams, or sleep disturbance alongside low mood and hopelessness all warrant
assessment beyond insomnia treatment.

[2] (condition-type-2-diabetes)
## What it is

Type 2 diabetes is a disorder of glucose regulation in which the body's tissues respond poorly to
insulin — insulin resistance — and the pancreas cannot sustain the increased output that resistance
demands. The result is a blood glucose level that stays above the normal range. It differs from type
1 diabetes, in which insulin-producing cells are destroyed by an autoimmune process and insulin is
absent rather than ineffective. The distinction matters because type 1 can present in adults, where
it is sometimes mislabeled.

The condition develops gradually, over years. The period of raised-but-not-diabetic glucose that
precedes it — prediabetes — is a recognized state with its own management, and it is the point at
which intensive lifestyle change has the largest effect.

## How it is usually recognized

Many people have no symptoms at diagnosis and are identified by screening. Where symptoms are
present, the classic ones are increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss,
fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds and recurrent infections. Because onset is gradual,
complications are sometimes already present at the time of diagnosis — which is the argument for
screening rather than waiting for symptoms.

Diagnostic thresholds and screening criteria are covered by the diabetes screening guideline note in
this corpus.

## What contributes to it

Excess body weight, particularly around the abdomen; physical inactivity; a family history of the
condition; increasing age; a history of gestational diabetes or of polycystic ovary syndrome; and
higher background risk in several racial and ethnic groups. Certain medications raise risk,
including long-term corticosteroids and some antipsychotics. Obstructive sleep apnea is commonly
present alongside it and worsens glucose control independently.

## Why it is treated

Sustained high glucose damages small and large blood vessels. The small-vessel complications are
retinal disease, kidney disease and nerve damage, including the foot problems that follow loss of
protective sensation. The large-vessel complications are heart attack, stroke and peripheral
arterial disease, which account for most of the excess mortality associated with the condition. Management therefore addresses blood pressure,
lipids and smoking alongside glucose, and modern treatment choices are made partly on cardiovascular
and kidney grounds rather than on glucose alone.

## How it is generally managed

Structured lifestyle intervention — dietary change, physical activity, weight management — together
with medication chosen according to which other conditions are present. Ongoing care includes
periodic measurement of long-term glucose control, annual eye screening, kidney function and urine
albumin testing, foot examination, and management of cardiovascular risk factors. Targets, testing
intervals and drug classes are covered by the diabetes guideline notes in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Very high glucose with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep or rapid breathing, drowsiness or
confusion may indicate a hyperglycemic emergency and requires immediate medical attention. Symptoms
of low blood sugar — shakiness, sweating, confusion, difficulty concentrating — in someone taking
insulin or an agent that stimulates insulin release require prompt treatment, and loss of
consciousness or seizure is an emergency. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these
situations.

[3] (condition-generalized-anxiety-disorder)
## What it is

Generalized anxiety disorder (generalised in British spelling) is persistent, excessive worry about
a range of everyday matters, occurring more days than not for at least six months, which the person
finds difficult to control and which is accompanied by physical and cognitive symptoms. The
distinguishing features are the breadth of the worry — it moves from topic to topic rather than
attaching to one situation — and the impairment it causes.

Anxiety itself is a normal and useful response to threat. What makes it a disorder is that it is
disproportionate to the circumstances, persistent when the circumstances change, and costly to
functioning.

## How it is usually recognized

The worry is accompanied by restlessness, being easily fatigued, difficulty concentrating,
irritability, muscle tension, and disturbed sleep. People frequently present with the physical
symptoms rather than the worry — palpitations, chest tightness, breathlessness, headaches,
gastrointestinal upset, dizziness — and are investigated for a physical cause first. That sequence is
appropriate the first time, since thyroid disease, arrhythmia, and stimulant or medication effects
genuinely produce these symptoms, but repeating it indefinitely delays the diagnosis.

Screening instruments and severity bands are covered by the anxiety guideline note in this corpus.

## What contributes to it

A combination of genetic predisposition, temperament, adverse childhood experience, chronic stress,
and physical illness. Caffeine, alcohol withdrawal, nicotine withdrawal, some medications, and
stimulant use can produce or worsen the symptoms, and they are worth reviewing before anything else
is concluded. Depression co-occurs frequently enough that finding one is a reason to assess for the
other, and the combination affects treatment choice.

## Why it is treated

Untreated, it tends to run a chronic, fluctuating course. It is associated with impaired work and
relationships, increased use of medical services and investigation, poorer outcomes in coexisting
physical illness, and increased risk of depression and substance use. It also responds well to
treatment — which is the more important point, since the condition's own logic tells the person that
nothing will help.

## How it is generally managed

Cognitive behavioral therapy or medication as first-line options of comparable effectiveness,
combined for more severe presentations, alongside sleep, activity, caffeine and alcohol review.
Self-management approaches with evidence include structured exercise, relaxation and mindfulness
practice, and guided digital programs. Treatment selection, review intervals and duration are
covered by the anxiety guideline note in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Thoughts of suicide or self-harm require urgent help rather than a routine appointment, and are
covered by the emergency notes in this corpus. A first panic attack with chest pain, breathlessness
or collapse is assessed as a physical emergency until a cardiac and respiratory cause has been
excluded — the two are not distinguishable by how they feel, and a person with an anxiety diagnosis
can also have a cardiac event.

[4] (condition-copd)
## What it is

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is persistent airflow limitation caused by long-term damage to
the airways and the lung tissue itself. Two processes usually coexist: chronic inflammation and
narrowing of the small airways, and emphysema, the destruction of the alveolar walls across which
gas is exchanged. The limitation is persistent rather than variable, which is the main contrast with
asthma, although the two overlap in some people and the overlap is treated as its own situation.

The damage is not reversible. Treatment reduces symptoms, improves exercise capacity and reduces
exacerbations; stopping the exposure that caused it is what changes the trajectory.

## How it is usually recognized

Breathlessness on exertion that has worsened gradually over years, chronic cough, and sputum
production, in someone with a relevant exposure history. People commonly attribute the early stage
to age or being out of shape and reduce their activity to match, which conceals the progression —
so the first presentation is often later than the first symptom, sometimes at an exacerbation.

The diagnosis requires spirometry and is not made on symptoms alone; the COPD guideline note in this
corpus covers the threshold and the assessment.

## What contributes to it

Tobacco smoking is the dominant cause in high-income countries. Also relevant: biomass fuel smoke
from indoor cooking and heating, occupational dust, vapors and fumes, air pollution, childhood
respiratory infections and impaired lung growth, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency — an inherited
condition worth considering when COPD appears young, in a non-smoker, or with a strong family
history.

## Exacerbations

An exacerbation is an acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond normal day-to-day variation,
usually triggered by a viral or bacterial infection. They matter more than the label suggests: each
one tends to worsen quality of life, accelerate lung-function decline, and predict the next, and a
history of them is the single strongest predictor of future ones. Recovery to baseline can take
weeks, and a proportion of people never return fully to their previous level.

## How it is generally managed

Smoking cessation above all; inhaled bronchodilator therapy, with inhaled corticosteroids where
indicated by exacerbations or eosinophil count; pulmonary rehabilitation; vaccination; assessment
for long-term oxygen therapy where resting oxygen levels are severely low; and a written plan for
what to do at an exacerbation. Nutrition, coexisting anxiety and depression, and treatable
comorbidities such as heart disease all affect symptoms and are managed alongside. The COPD
guideline note in this corpus covers therapy selection and review intervals.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Worsening breathlessness that does not respond to the usual reliever, breathlessness at rest,
confusion or unusual drowsiness, blue discoloration of the lips or fingers, chest pain, coughing
blood, or a fever with a marked change in sputum — these need urgent assessment rather than a
routine appointment. Drowsiness in someone struggling to breathe is a particularly serious sign,
because it can indicate rising carbon dioxide rather than tiredness. The emergency-symptom notes in
this corpus govern these situations.

[5] (condition-gerd)
## What it is

Gastroesophageal reflux disease — gastro-oesophageal in British spelling, and abbreviated GERD or
GORD accordingly — is the condition in which stomach contents move back into the esophagus often
enough, or with enough consequence, to cause troublesome symptoms or damage to the esophageal
lining. Some reflux is normal and happens in everyone; what makes it a disease is the symptom burden
or the injury, not the presence of reflux itself.

The usual mechanism is transient relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, the ring of muscle at
the junction between esophagus (oesophagus) and stomach, sometimes with a hiatus hernia that
displaces the junction and weakens the barrier further.

## How it is usually recognized

The typical symptoms are heartburn — a burning discomfort rising behind the breastbone — and
regurgitation of acid or food into the throat, often worse after meals, on bending forward, and when
lying down. The pattern, particularly its relation to meals and position, is more informative than
the severity.

Less typical presentations include chronic cough, hoarseness, throat clearing, a sensation of a lump
in the throat, dental erosion, and non-cardiac chest pain. These are considerably less specific:
many people with them turn out to have another explanation, which is why attributing them to reflux
without considering alternatives is unreliable and why they respond less predictably to acid
suppression.

## What contributes to it

Excess body weight, particularly abdominal; hiatus hernia; pregnancy; smoking; large or late meals;
and alcohol. Several medications can worsen it, including calcium-channel blockers, nitrates and
others that relax the lower esophageal sphincter. Individual food triggers vary and are far less
consistent between people than is usually assumed, which is the argument for identifying a person's
own triggers rather than applying a standard list.

## Why it is treated

Beyond symptom burden, which can be substantial and affects sleep and quality of life, persistent
acid exposure can cause esophagitis, stricture with narrowing and difficulty swallowing, and
Barrett's esophagus — a change in the lining that carries a small increased risk of esophageal
cancer. That risk is the reason long-standing or alarm-feature-associated reflux is investigated
rather than treated indefinitely on assumption.

## How it is generally managed

Weight management where relevant, meal timing and portion changes, elevating the head of the bed for
night-time symptoms, smoking cessation, and acid-suppressing treatment with a defined trial period
and reassessment rather than open-ended use. Alarm features, endoscopy indications and the step-down
approach are covered by the GERD guideline note in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Chest discomfort must not be assumed to be reflux. Discomfort brought on by exertion, or coming with
breathlessness, sweating, nausea, or pain spreading to the arm, neck or jaw, or occurring in someone
with cardiovascular risk factors, requires emergency assessment for a cardiac cause first —
heartburn and cardiac pain are not reliably distinguishable by how they feel. Difficulty swallowing,
painful swallowing, vomiting blood, black tarry stools, or unintentional weight loss also require
prompt medical assessment. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

question: How long does a common cold usually last?
answer:
A common cold typically lasts about seven to ten days. This duration is considered normal for an upper respiratory infection caused by a virus. While symptoms might improve as the days progress, a cough can persist for a bit longer, up to two to three weeks, even after the other symptoms have resolved (Infectious diseases society and public health antimicrobial stewardship guidance).

Management of a common cold mainly involves supportive care, such as rest and staying hydrated. It is important to note that antibiotics are not effective against viral infections like the common cold, and thus are not recommended for treatment (General clinical reference).

[1] (guideline-uri-antibiotic-stewardship)
## The default position

Acute upper respiratory infections — the common cold, most sore throats, acute bronchitis, and
uncomplicated acute sinusitis in its first days — are viral in the large majority of cases, and
antibiotics do not shorten them, do not prevent complications at a rate that justifies routine use,
and do cause harm: adverse effects, allergic reactions, disruption of normal flora, *Clostridioides
difficile* infection, and selection for resistant organisms in the individual as well as the
population.

Guidance describes not prescribing antibiotics for these presentations as the active recommendation,
not merely the absence of one. Communication is treated as part of the clinical intervention:
explaining the expected course, naming the duration, describing what would change the plan, and
offering symptomatic measures reduces both prescribing and dissatisfaction, whereas a bare refusal
does neither.

## What does not indicate a bacterial infection

- **Discolored nasal discharge.** Yellow or green discharge is part of the normal viral course.
- **Duration alone within the expected window.** A cold lasting seven to ten days is running its
  course; cough alone persisting two to three weeks after a cold is expected.
- **Low-grade fever** in the first days.
- **Productive cough** in acute bronchitis, which is viral in the overwhelming majority of
  otherwise healthy adults.

## When antibiotics are described as indicated

- **Acute bacterial sinusitis**, identified by one of three patterns rather than by symptoms alone:
  symptoms persisting ten days or more without improvement; severe symptoms with high fever and
  purulent discharge for three to four consecutive days at onset; or the "double worsening" pattern
  in which symptoms improve and then deteriorate.
- **Group A streptococcal pharyngitis**, confirmed by rapid antigen testing or culture rather than
  by appearance. Clinical scoring systems select who to test; they do not replace the test, since
  the features overlap heavily with viral pharyngitis.
- **Pneumonia**, suspected on focal findings, abnormal vital signs, or a compatible chest image —
  a different diagnosis rather than an upper respiratory infection that has gone on too long.
- **Complications** such as peritonsillar abscess, or infection in someone significantly
  immunocompromised.

## Delayed prescribing

A prescription given with instructions to fill it only if symptoms fail to improve or worsen by a
stated point is described as a middle option, reducing antibiotic use substantially compared with
immediate prescribing while maintaining satisfaction. It is described as most useful where the
clinician judges bacterial infection unlikely but the person's expectation or access to follow-up
argues against a plain refusal.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on how far the delayed-prescription strategy should be encouraged. Some describe it as
a recommended tool for reducing immediate prescribing; others are wary, on the grounds that it still
results in a prescription in a substantial fraction of cases and may reinforce the expectation that
these illnesses warrant antibiotics at all. Guidance also differs on sore-throat management, with
some national guidance placing greater weight on clinical scoring and less on universal testing
before treatment.

[2] (condition-upper-respiratory-infection)
## What it is

An upper respiratory infection is a viral infection of the nose, sinuses, throat and upper airway.
Rhinoviruses cause the largest share; coronaviruses, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza,
adenovirus and others account for the rest. It is self-limiting in the great majority of otherwise
healthy people.

The distinction from influenza is clinically useful. A cold begins gradually, is dominated by nasal
symptoms and sore throat, and rarely produces high fever or prostration in adults. Influenza
typically begins abruptly with fever, muscle aches and marked malaise, with respiratory symptoms
following. The distinction is not reliable enough to be certain in an individual, but it usefully
shifts the probability.

## How it is usually recognized

Nasal congestion and discharge, sneezing, sore throat, cough, mild headache and malaise, sometimes a
low-grade fever. Symptoms typically peak at two to three days and resolve over seven to ten days.
Cough frequently outlasts everything else, persisting two to three weeks, which is normal and not by
itself evidence of a bacterial infection or of treatment failure.

Discharge changing from clear to yellow or green is part of the normal course, reflecting immune
cells rather than bacterial infection. This is the single most common reason people seek antibiotics
for a cold, and it is not an indication for them.

## What contributes to it

Exposure to infected people, which is why incidence rises with young children in the household and
in the colder months when people are indoors. Transmission is by respiratory droplets and by
contaminated hands and surfaces reaching the eyes or nose. Hand hygiene reduces transmission
measurably; the belief that cold exposure itself causes colds does not survive examination.

## How it is generally managed

Supportive care: rest, fluids, and symptomatic relief. Antibiotics have no effect on viral infection
and carry real harms — adverse effects, disruption of normal flora, and antimicrobial resistance —
which is why antibiotic stewardship for these presentations is an explicit guideline topic rather
than a matter of preference. Over-the-counter symptomatic treatments have modest effects on symptoms
and none on duration, and several are not appropriate for young children.

## When further assessment is advised

Symptoms worsening after an initial improvement, fever returning after it had settled, symptoms
persisting beyond ten days without improvement, severe facial pain or one-sided facial swelling,
severe sore throat with difficulty swallowing or drooling, or breathlessness — these suggest a
complication such as bacterial sinusitis, pneumonia, or a throat infection needing assessment.

People at higher risk of complications — infants, older adults, pregnancy, and anyone with chronic
lung, heart, kidney or liver disease, diabetes, or a weakened immune system — warrant earlier
assessment than an otherwise healthy adult.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Difficulty breathing, chest pain, a stiff neck with severe headache, confusion, persistent vomiting
preventing fluid intake, or signs of dehydration require urgent assessment. The emergency-symptom
notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[3] (condition-asthma)
## What it is

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory condition of the airways in which the airway lining is inflamed and
the surrounding muscle is prone to constrict, producing airflow obstruction that varies over time
and is at least partly reversible. The variability is the defining feature: lung function and
symptoms change from day to day and within a day. That distinguishes it from the persistent
obstruction of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, although the two can coexist, and the
combination is more common in older people with a smoking history.

## How it is usually recognized

The characteristic pattern is wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough that vary in
intensity, are often worse at night or in the early morning, and are provoked by identifiable
triggers. Cough alone, particularly at night, is a recognized presentation and is often attributed
to something else for a long time before the pattern is noticed. Symptoms that are entirely constant,
or that never respond to a bronchodilator, prompt consideration of an alternative explanation.

Objective evidence of variable airflow limitation is required as well as the symptom pattern; the
asthma guideline note in this corpus covers it.

## Common triggers

Viral respiratory infections, house dust mite, pollen, animal dander, mold, tobacco smoke, air
pollution, cold air, exercise, strong odors, occupational exposures, and certain medications —
including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and beta-blockers in susceptible people. Emotional
stress and laughter can precipitate symptoms, which is not the same as the condition being
psychological in origin. Identifying an individual's triggers is part of management, since avoidance
where practical reduces the treatment burden; occupational asthma is worth identifying early,
because it can remit if the exposure ends soon enough.

## Control and severity are different things

This distinction matters and is frequently confused. **Control** describes how much the condition is
currently affecting the person — daytime symptoms, night waking, reliever use, and activity
limitation — and can change within weeks. **Severity** describes how much treatment is required to
achieve control, and is assessed retrospectively once treatment is established. Poor control is
usually a treatment, adherence or inhaler-technique problem rather than evidence of severe disease,
and treating it as severity leads to escalation where a technique check was needed.

## How it is generally managed

Regular anti-inflammatory inhaled therapy, a reliever, trigger avoidance where practical, inhaler
technique training, a written action plan describing what to do when symptoms worsen, and treatment
of contributing conditions such as allergic rhinitis, reflux and obesity. Stepwise treatment
structure and review intervals are covered by the asthma guideline note in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

An attack that does not respond to reliever treatment, or that returns within a few hours, requires
prompt medical assessment. Immediate emergency attention is advised for difficulty speaking in full
sentences, breathlessness at rest, drowsiness or confusion, blue discoloration of the lips or
fingers, or a chest that has become quiet because too little air is moving to produce a wheeze — the
absence of wheeze during a severe attack is a serious sign, not a reassuring one. The
emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[4] (condition-influenza)
## What it is

Influenza is a respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses, of which types A and B cause
seasonal epidemics. Influenza A is subtyped by two surface proteins, hemagglutinin and
neuraminidase — the H and N in designations such as H1N1 and H3N2. The virus changes continuously
through small mutations, which is why immunity from one season is incomplete against the next and
why the vaccine is reformulated annually rather than given once.

It is more severe than a common cold in both symptoms and consequences, and it causes substantial
seasonal hospitalization and death, concentrated in older adults, young children, pregnant people
and those with chronic conditions.

## How it is usually recognized

Abrupt onset — people can often name the hour — with fever, chills, muscle aches, headache, marked
fatigue and dry cough. Sore throat and nasal symptoms occur but are less prominent than in a cold.
Fever typically lasts three to five days; cough and fatigue commonly persist two weeks or more.
Gastrointestinal symptoms occur more often in children than adults.

Laboratory confirmation is not required to manage a typical case during a known outbreak, and is
used where the result would change management — in hospital, in high-risk people, or where an
antiviral decision or outbreak control depends on it.

## Complications

Pneumonia is the main one, either from the virus itself or from a secondary bacterial infection.
Secondary bacterial pneumonia classically appears as a deterioration after several days of
improvement, which is a pattern worth recognizing. Other complications include worsening of
underlying asthma, COPD, heart failure or diabetes, and less commonly inflammation of the heart
muscle, brain or muscle tissue. Influenza is also associated with a transient increase in the risk
of myocardial infarction and stroke in the weeks after infection.

## How it is generally managed

Supportive care for most otherwise healthy people: rest, fluids, and symptomatic relief. Antiviral
treatment is targeted rather than universal, and is most effective when started early — the timing
threshold and the groups in whom treatment is recommended are covered by the influenza guideline
note in this corpus. Antibiotics have no effect on the virus and are reserved for a bacterial
complication.

Annual vaccination is the principal preventive measure, alongside staying home while febrile, hand
hygiene and respiratory etiquette.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Difficulty breathing or breathlessness at rest, chest pain, persistent dizziness or confusion,
inability to keep fluids down, seizures, severe muscle pain or weakness, or symptoms that improve
and then return with fever and worse cough — these need urgent assessment. In children, additional
signs include fast or labored breathing, blue lips, no tears when crying, and significantly reduced
wet diapers. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[5] (guideline-coronary-artery-disease-secondary-prevention)
## What secondary prevention means

Secondary prevention is the set of measures used for someone who already has established coronary
artery disease — a previous heart attack, a revascularization procedure, or angiographic disease —
to reduce the chance of a further event. It is a package rather than a single intervention: no one
element carries the effect, and the benefit measured in trials comes from applying them together.
Partial application is the common failure, and it is usually the non-drug elements that are dropped.

## The components

- **Antiplatelet therapy** — long-term single antiplatelet therapy for most people, with a defined
  period of dual antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome or stent placement, its
  duration individualized against bleeding risk.
- **High-intensity statin therapy**. United States guidance describes the intensity; European
  guidance describes an LDL goal instead. Where the response is inadequate, additional
  non-statin agents are added rather than the statin abandoned.
- **Blood-pressure control**, with a target below 130/80 mm Hg for most people.
- **Renin-angiotensin blockade** where diabetes, reduced left ventricular function, or chronic
  kidney disease is also present.
- **Beta-blockade** after myocardial infarction, with the strongest and longest-standing evidence
  where left ventricular function is reduced.
- **Cardiac rehabilitation referral** — a structured program of supervised exercise, education and
  risk-factor management, and consistently one of the most underused elements relative to the
  strength of the evidence behind it.
- **Smoking cessation**, the single largest modifiable factor, with combined behavioral and
  pharmacologic support more effective than advice alone.
- **Annual influenza vaccination**, included as a cardiovascular measure rather than only a
  respiratory one.
- **Structured management of diabetes** where present, preferring agents with demonstrated
  cardiovascular benefit.

## Review interval

Review at least annually once the regimen is stable, with earlier review after any change in
symptoms, after a hospital admission, and four to twelve weeks after any change in lipid-lowering
intensity. Each review is an opportunity to check adherence, which falls measurably in the year
after an event as the acute experience recedes.

## What warrants urgent reassessment

New, worsening, or rest-onset chest discomfort in someone with known coronary disease is not a
routine review matter and requires urgent assessment. A pattern of angina that is becoming more
frequent, more easily provoked, or longer-lasting is a change in category rather than a change in
degree. The emergency-symptom notes elsewhere in this corpus govern these situations, and this note
does not substitute for them.

question: How is blood pressure actually measured, and why is more than one reading needed?
answer:
Blood pressure is measured using a sphygmomanometer, which involves inflating a cuff around the upper arm and then slowly releasing the air while listening for heartbeats. The pressure is recorded as two numbers: the systolic pressure (when the heart beats) over the diastolic pressure (when the heart is at rest). Both measurements are expressed in millimeters of mercury (mmHg).

Taking multiple readings is important because blood pressure can vary significantly due to factors like activity, stress, and time of day. A single high reading isn’t enough for diagnosis. Instead, a diagnosis of hypertension requires consistently elevated blood pressure readings over time. This helps ensure that the measurement reflects a person’s typical blood pressure rather than a temporary spike due to circumstances such as anxiety during a medical visit (from "Hypertension (high blood pressure)"). 

This variability is why many healthcare guidelines recommend multiple measurements to obtain an accurate assessment of blood pressure.

[1] (condition-hypertension)
## What it is

Hypertension is persistently raised pressure in the arteries, sustained over time rather than on a
single occasion. Blood pressure is written as two numbers: the systolic pressure, generated when the
heart contracts, over the diastolic pressure, present between beats. Both are measured in
millimeters of mercury.

Pressure varies continuously through the day — with activity, stress, pain, caffeine, sleep and time
of day, typically lowest during sleep and rising before waking. That variation is why a diagnosis
rests on repeated measurements rather than one reading, and why a single high reading in a clinic is
not itself a diagnosis.

## How it is usually recognized

Hypertension is typically without symptoms and is most often found on routine measurement rather
than because someone felt unwell. That is the main reason screening for it exists at all. Where
symptoms such as headache, visual disturbance or nosebleed are attributed to raised blood pressure,
they usually reflect either a very high pressure or an unrelated cause — the belief that ordinary
hypertension can be felt leads people to treat by symptom rather than by measurement, which does not
work.

## What contributes to it

Most cases have no single identifiable cause and reflect a combination of age, genetic
predisposition, excess body weight, high dietary sodium, low potassium intake, physical inactivity,
alcohol intake, poor sleep including untreated sleep apnea (apnoea), and chronic stress. Arterial
stiffening with age is why systolic pressure tends to rise across the lifespan while diastolic
pressure often falls after middle age.

A minority of cases have an identifiable secondary cause — kidney disease, renal artery narrowing,
primary aldosteronism, thyroid or adrenal disorders, obstructive sleep apnea, and certain medications
including combined oral contraceptives, decongestants, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and
some stimulants. Investigation for a secondary cause is usually considered when hypertension appears
at a young age, is unusually severe, responds poorly to treatment, or worsens abruptly after a period
of stability.

## Why it is treated

Sustained high pressure damages arteries over years, and the conditions that follow are the reason
for treating a symptomless number: stroke, heart attack, heart failure, chronic kidney disease,
retinal damage, and cognitive decline. The benefit of treatment is measured in reduced rates of those
events, not in how the person feels — which is also why adherence is difficult, since a treatment
that produces no felt improvement and occasional side effects is easy to stop.

## How it is generally managed

Lifestyle measures — dietary sodium reduction, a diet pattern high in vegetables, fruit and whole
grains, regular activity, weight management, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking — apply to
everyone. Drug treatment is added according to the level of risk. Diagnostic thresholds, treatment
targets, drug classes and follow-up intervals are covered by the hypertension guideline notes in
this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

A very high reading accompanied by chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, visual loss,
confusion, weakness or numbness on one side, or difficulty speaking is an emergency and requires
immediate medical attention rather than a routine appointment. The emergency-symptom notes in this
corpus govern those situations.

[2] (condition-heart-failure)
## What it is

Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart cannot fill with or eject blood well enough
to meet the body's needs at normal filling pressures. The name is misleading in a way worth
correcting: it does not mean the heart has stopped or is about to. It is a chronic condition that is
managed, often for many years.

It is classified by ejection fraction — the proportion of blood in the left ventricle expelled with
each beat — because the evidence for treatment differs sharply between the groups: reduced (40
percent or below), mildly reduced (41 to 49 percent), and preserved (50 percent or above). Preserved
ejection fraction accounts for roughly half of cases and is not a milder form; it is a different
problem, one of stiffness and impaired filling rather than weak contraction.

## How it is usually recognized

Breathlessness on exertion, then at lower levels of exertion, then when lying flat; waking at night
breathless; swelling of the ankles and legs; fatigue; reduced exercise tolerance; and weight gain
over days that reflects retained fluid rather than tissue. Distinguishing fluid weight from other
weight change matters, because a rise of two or three kilograms across a few days is a fluid signal
and a reason to act.

Confirming the diagnosis involves natriuretic peptide blood testing and echocardiography, which
establishes the ejection fraction that determines the treatment pathway.

## What contributes to it

Coronary artery disease and previous myocardial infarction are the most common causes, followed by
long-standing high blood pressure. Also: valve disease, atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathies
including genetic and post-viral forms, alcohol, some chemotherapy agents, thyroid disease, and
iron overload. Diabetes, obesity, chronic kidney disease and sleep apnea (apnoea) commonly coexist
and worsen the course.

## Why it is treated

Treatment reduces symptoms, hospital admissions and mortality. Modern therapy for reduced ejection
fraction has changed the outlook substantially, and a proportion of people recover ventricular
function on it — which is why the ejection fraction is reassessed after therapy is established
rather than treated as a fixed property. The four foundational classes and their titration are
covered by the heart-failure guideline note in this corpus.

## How it is generally managed

Disease-modifying drug therapy according to ejection fraction; diuretics for congestion; treating
the underlying cause and the coexisting conditions; devices in selected people; cardiac
rehabilitation; vaccination; and structured self-management — daily weights, recognizing early
fluid retention, and knowing when to seek help. Sodium and fluid advice is individualized rather
than uniform.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Breathlessness at rest or that wakes the person and does not settle when upright, chest pain, rapid
weight gain over a few days, fainting, a very fast or irregular pulse with symptoms, or confusion —
these need urgent assessment. Pink frothy sputum with severe breathlessness is an emergency. The
emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[3] (condition-coronary-artery-disease)
## What it is

Coronary artery disease is the build-up of atherosclerotic plaque in the arteries supplying the
heart muscle. Plaque develops over decades, beginning with injury to the artery lining and the
accumulation of cholesterol-rich material beneath it. Two distinct mechanisms produce symptoms, and
confusing them is the source of most misunderstanding about the condition:

- **Gradual narrowing** limits blood flow when demand rises, producing predictable exertional chest
  discomfort — stable angina.
- **Plaque rupture** exposes material that triggers clot formation, which can occlude the artery
  abruptly. This produces an acute coronary syndrome, and it can happen at a plaque that was never
  narrow enough to cause symptoms. That is why a normal stress test in the past does not mean a
  heart attack cannot happen now.

## How it is usually recognized

Stable angina is classically a pressure, tightness or heaviness in the chest, brought on by exertion
or emotional stress, relieved within minutes by rest, and sometimes spreading to the arm, neck, jaw
or back. It is a reproducible pattern — the same amount of effort brings it on.

Presentations are frequently not classical. Breathlessness on exertion without chest discomfort,
unusual fatigue, nausea, or discomfort felt mainly in the jaw, back or upper abdomen are all
recognized presentations, and are relatively more common in women, older people, and people with
diabetes, in whom nerve damage can blunt the pain. The consequence is delayed presentation, and the
delay is what causes the harm.

## What contributes to it

Smoking, high blood pressure, raised LDL cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, a diet
high in saturated fat and low in vegetables and fiber, chronic kidney disease, inflammatory
conditions, and a family history of premature coronary disease. Age and male sex raise baseline risk
and cannot be modified; the rest of the list can be, which is what makes the risk estimate
actionable rather than merely descriptive.

## Why it is treated

Untreated coronary disease leads to myocardial infarction, heart failure from damaged muscle,
arrhythmia, and death. Secondary prevention after a diagnosis substantially reduces the rate of
further events, and the effect comes from the package rather than from any single element — covered
by the secondary-prevention guideline note in this corpus.

## How it is generally managed

Risk-factor treatment, antiplatelet and lipid-lowering therapy, agents to control angina symptoms,
cardiac rehabilitation, and revascularization — stenting or bypass surgery — where symptoms persist
despite medical therapy or where the pattern of disease indicates it. Revascularization relieves
symptoms reliably; it does not remove the need for the medical therapy underneath.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Chest discomfort at rest, discomfort lasting more than a few minutes, discomfort with breathlessness,
sweating, nausea or light-headedness, or angina that is newly more frequent or more easily provoked
— these are emergencies and need immediate medical attention rather than a routine appointment.
Waiting to see whether it settles is the most common and most costly error. The emergency-symptom
notes in this corpus govern these situations.

[4] (condition-type-2-diabetes)
## What it is

Type 2 diabetes is a disorder of glucose regulation in which the body's tissues respond poorly to
insulin — insulin resistance — and the pancreas cannot sustain the increased output that resistance
demands. The result is a blood glucose level that stays above the normal range. It differs from type
1 diabetes, in which insulin-producing cells are destroyed by an autoimmune process and insulin is
absent rather than ineffective. The distinction matters because type 1 can present in adults, where
it is sometimes mislabeled.

The condition develops gradually, over years. The period of raised-but-not-diabetic glucose that
precedes it — prediabetes — is a recognized state with its own management, and it is the point at
which intensive lifestyle change has the largest effect.

## How it is usually recognized

Many people have no symptoms at diagnosis and are identified by screening. Where symptoms are
present, the classic ones are increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss,
fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds and recurrent infections. Because onset is gradual,
complications are sometimes already present at the time of diagnosis — which is the argument for
screening rather than waiting for symptoms.

Diagnostic thresholds and screening criteria are covered by the diabetes screening guideline note in
this corpus.

## What contributes to it

Excess body weight, particularly around the abdomen; physical inactivity; a family history of the
condition; increasing age; a history of gestational diabetes or of polycystic ovary syndrome; and
higher background risk in several racial and ethnic groups. Certain medications raise risk,
including long-term corticosteroids and some antipsychotics. Obstructive sleep apnea is commonly
present alongside it and worsens glucose control independently.

## Why it is treated

Sustained high glucose damages small and large blood vessels. The small-vessel complications are
retinal disease, kidney disease and nerve damage, including the foot problems that follow loss of
protective sensation. The large-vessel complications are heart attack, stroke and peripheral
arterial disease, which account for most of the excess mortality associated with the condition. Management therefore addresses blood pressure,
lipids and smoking alongside glucose, and modern treatment choices are made partly on cardiovascular
and kidney grounds rather than on glucose alone.

## How it is generally managed

Structured lifestyle intervention — dietary change, physical activity, weight management — together
with medication chosen according to which other conditions are present. Ongoing care includes
periodic measurement of long-term glucose control, annual eye screening, kidney function and urine
albumin testing, foot examination, and management of cardiovascular risk factors. Targets, testing
intervals and drug classes are covered by the diabetes guideline notes in this corpus.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Very high glucose with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep or rapid breathing, drowsiness or
confusion may indicate a hyperglycemic emergency and requires immediate medical attention. Symptoms
of low blood sugar — shakiness, sweating, confusion, difficulty concentrating — in someone taking
insulin or an agent that stimulates insulin release require prompt treatment, and loss of
consciousness or seizure is an emergency. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus govern these
situations.

[5] (condition-iron-deficiency-anemia)
## What it is

Anemia (anaemia in British spelling) is a reduced concentration of hemoglobin (haemoglobin), the
oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells. Iron deficiency is its most common cause worldwide. Iron
is required to make hemoglobin, so when body iron stores are exhausted, red cells are produced
smaller and paler than normal — the microcytic, hypochromic pattern seen on a blood count.

The critical point about iron-deficiency anemia in adults is that it is a **finding, not a
diagnosis**. Iron is not lost from the body in significant amounts except through bleeding, so
deficiency in an adult who is not menstruating heavily or pregnant raises the question of where the
iron went. Treating the anemia without answering that question can leave a gastrointestinal cancer
undetected, which is the reason the workup exists.

## How it is usually recognized

Fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, breathlessness on exertion, palpitations, headache, dizziness,
pale skin, cold hands and feet, brittle nails, and hair thinning. Less familiar features that are
relatively specific to iron deficiency include restless legs and pica — craving non-food substances,
classically ice.

Onset is usually gradual, and the body compensates well, so people frequently attribute months of
increasing fatigue to their circumstances and present only when compensation fails. Anemia is often
found incidentally on a blood count taken for another reason.

## Establishing the cause

The blood count shows the pattern; ferritin is the primary test of iron stores, with the caveat that
it rises in inflammation and can therefore appear normal despite deficiency, in which case
transferrin saturation and other iron studies clarify it. Once deficiency is confirmed, the source
is investigated: menstrual and pregnancy history, dietary intake, medications including
anti-inflammatories and anticoagulants, celiac serology, and — where no adequate explanation exists,
particularly in men and post-menopausal women — investigation of the gastrointestinal tract.

## What contributes to it

Blood loss: heavy menstrual bleeding, gastrointestinal bleeding from ulcers, inflammatory disease,
polyps or cancer, and frequent blood donation. Increased requirement: pregnancy, breastfeeding,
infancy and adolescence. Reduced absorption: celiac disease, previous gastric surgery, *Helicobacter
pylori* infection, and long-term acid suppression. Inadequate intake, which is a sufficient
explanation more often in restricted diets and in children than in adults.

## How it is generally managed

Correcting the underlying cause, together with iron replacement — oral in most cases, intravenous
where oral is not tolerated, not absorbed, or where correction needs to be rapid. Replacement
continues after the hemoglobin normalizes in order to refill stores, which is the step most often
stopped too early, and the response is confirmed by repeat testing rather than assumed. Doses are
outside the scope of this system.

## When urgent assessment is advised

Chest pain, breathlessness at rest, fainting, a rapid heart rate at rest, or vomiting blood or
passing black tarry stools require urgent assessment. The emergency-symptom notes in this corpus
govern these situations.

question: What sort of dietary change does guidance describe for high blood pressure?
answer:
Guidance on dietary changes for managing high blood pressure emphasizes several lifestyle measures:

1. **Reduce Dietary Sodium**: Lowering salt intake is consistently recommended to help manage blood pressure.
  
2. **Adopt a Healthy Dietary Pattern**: This includes a diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products while being low in saturated fats.

3. **Regular Aerobic Activity**: Engaging in regular exercise, such as aerobic activity most days of the week, is beneficial.

4. **Weight Management**: Achieving and maintaining a healthy body weight is important.

5. **Limit Alcohol and Stop Smoking**: Reducing alcohol intake and quitting smoking are also recommended lifestyle changes.

These recommendations are part of a broad set of non-drug measures advocated by major health organizations, which indicate that each of these changes can contribute to lowering blood pressure, and their effects may be additive when combined (source: “Hypertension: when treatment starts and which options are first-line”).

[1] (guideline-hypertension-first-line-treatment)
## Lifestyle measures are the shared foundation

Every major body recommends the same set of non-drug measures, whether or not medication is also
used: reducing dietary sodium, adopting a dietary pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains
and low-fat dairy and low in saturated fat, regular aerobic activity most days of the week, weight
reduction where body weight is above the healthy range, limiting alcohol, and stopping smoking.
Each produces a meaningful reduction on its own, and the effects are partly additive, so several
combined can move a person a full stage.

## When drug treatment starts

The decision is tied to cardiovascular risk, not to the blood-pressure number alone:

- **Stage 2 hypertension** — drug treatment alongside lifestyle measures, usually beginning with
  two agents, because a single agent rarely closes a gap of this size.
- **Stage 1 hypertension with established cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney
  disease, or an estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk at or above 10 percent** — drug treatment
  alongside lifestyle measures.
- **Stage 1 hypertension without those features** — lifestyle measures first, with reassessment
  after three to six months before drug treatment is considered.

## First-line drug classes

Four classes are first-line for most adults without a compelling indication for something else:
thiazide-type diuretics, angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers,
and dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers. An ACE inhibitor and an angiotensin receptor blocker
are not combined — the combination adds harm without adding benefit. Single-pill combinations are
preferred where two agents are needed, because adherence falls as pill count rises.

Comorbidity shifts the choice. Renin-angiotensin blockade is preferred where diabetes with
albuminuria or chronic kidney disease is present; a beta-blocker is not first-line for uncomplicated
hypertension but becomes appropriate where there is a separate indication such as heart failure or
recent myocardial infarction. Doses are outside the scope of this note and of this system.

## Resistant hypertension

Blood pressure above target on three agents including a diuretic, all at appropriate doses, is
described as resistant hypertension. Before treatment is escalated further, the sequence is to
confirm the readings out of office, review adherence, review agents that raise blood pressure —
non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, decongestants, some stimulants, combined oral contraceptives
— and investigate for a secondary cause. Apparent resistance is more often measurement, adherence
or an interfering agent than a need for a fourth drug.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on how aggressively to treat low-risk stage 1 hypertension, which follows from the
threshold disagreement in the diagnostic note: where guidance describes hypertension as beginning at
140/90 mm Hg, much of the population that United States guidance calls stage 1 is instead advised on
lifestyle alone.

## Follow-up interval

Monthly review until the target is reached, including adherence and a check of kidney function and
potassium after starting an agent acting on the renin-angiotensin system, then review every three
to six months once stable.

[2] (guideline-hypertension-diagnosis-and-bp-targets)
## What this guidance covers

How adult office blood pressure is classified, what is required before a diagnosis of hypertension
is made, and the treatment target most bodies set once treatment has begun.

## Classification of office blood pressure in adults

United States society guidance classifies adult office readings as:

- **Normal** — systolic below 120 mm Hg *and* diastolic below 80 mm Hg.
- **Elevated** — systolic 120 to 129 mm Hg *and* diastolic below 80 mm Hg.
- **Stage 1 hypertension** — systolic 130 to 139 mm Hg *or* diastolic 80 to 89 mm Hg.
- **Stage 2 hypertension** — systolic at least 140 mm Hg *or* diastolic at least 90 mm Hg.

When the systolic and diastolic values fall into different categories, the higher category applies.
"Elevated" is not a stage of hypertension: it marks a group at raised future risk in whom lifestyle
measures are advised and drug treatment is not.

## Measurement technique, which changes the number

A reading taken carelessly is not a milder version of a correct reading — it is a different
measurement. The technique that the classification above assumes is a validated device, a cuff
sized to the arm, the person seated with back supported and feet flat, arm supported at heart
level, no caffeine, exercise or smoking in the preceding 30 minutes, five minutes of rest
beforehand, and no talking during the measurement. An undersized cuff and an unsupported arm both
push the reading up, each by an amount comparable to the width of a whole stage.

## Confirming the diagnosis

A diagnosis is not made from a single reading. The standard is an average of two or more readings
taken on two or more separate occasions. Out-of-office measurement — home readings or 24-hour
ambulatory monitoring — confirms the diagnosis and identifies two patterns that office readings
alone cannot: white-coat hypertension, where office readings are raised but out-of-office readings
are not, and masked hypertension, where the reverse holds and the risk is underestimated.

## Treatment target

For most treated adults, United States guidance describes a target below 130/80 mm Hg. The target is
individualized for older adults with frailty, limited life expectancy, or a heavy burden of other
conditions, where the balance of benefit and harm differs and where postural drops matter more.

## Where guidance differs

The 130/80 mm Hg diagnostic threshold is a United States position. European guidance describes office
hypertension as beginning at 140/90 mm Hg, and treats the 130 to 139 / 80 to 89 band as high-normal
blood pressure rather than as stage 1 disease. The same reading is therefore labeled differently
depending on which body's guidance is applied, and the size of the population called hypertensive
changes substantially between the two. Any answer that quotes a threshold should say which
convention it is using.

## Follow-up interval

After treatment starts or changes, reassessment at roughly monthly intervals until the target is
reached, then review every three to six months once readings are stable.

[3] (guideline-lipid-screening-and-statin-initiation)
## Screening

The screening test is a lipid panel — total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and
triglycerides. A non-fasting sample is acceptable for initial screening in most adults; a fasting
sample is preferred where triglycerides are markedly raised, since the triglyceride value and the
calculated LDL derived from it are the parts most affected by a recent meal.

The usual screening interval is every four to six years for adults aged 20 to 75 who are at low risk
and not on lipid-lowering therapy, and shorter where risk factors are present or where risk is being
reassessed before a treatment decision.

## Risk stratification

The central move in current guidance is that the decision is driven by estimated 10-year
atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk, not by the LDL number alone. Risk is estimated from age, sex,
race, total and HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, treatment for hypertension, diabetes and
smoking status. The four named risk categories, for adults aged 40 to 75 without established
disease, are:

- **Low** — estimated 10-year risk below 5 percent.
- **Borderline** — 5 percent to below 7.5 percent.
- **Intermediate** — 7.5 percent to below 20 percent.
- **High** — 20 percent or above.

Risk-enhancing features shift a decision within the borderline and intermediate bands rather than
replacing the estimate: family history of premature cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease,
chronic inflammatory conditions, persistently raised triglycerides, metabolic syndrome, conditions
specific to pregnancy such as pre-eclampsia, and, where the decision remains uncertain, a coronary
artery calcium score.

## Groups in which therapy is indicated

- **Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease** — high-intensity statin therapy as
  secondary prevention.
- **LDL cholesterol at or above 190 mg/dL** — high-intensity statin therapy regardless of the
  calculated risk score, which is not designed for this group.
- **Diabetes, aged 40 to 75** — at least moderate-intensity statin therapy.
- **Intermediate risk** — moderate-intensity statin therapy after a risk discussion.
- **Borderline risk** — guidance describes a risk discussion rather than a default action, with
  therapy favored where risk-enhancing features are present and reasonably deferred where they are
  not.

## Monitoring interval

The lipid panel is repeated four to twelve weeks after starting therapy or changing intensity, which
assesses response and adherence together, then every three to twelve months once stable. Routine
liver enzyme monitoring is not part of ongoing care in the absence of symptoms; a baseline
measurement is usual.

## Where guidance differs

Bodies differ on whether to state numeric LDL targets. United States guidance describes statin
intensity and percentage reduction from baseline; European guidance describes explicit LDL goals
that fall as risk category rises, pursued with combination therapy where a statin alone falls short. Answers should say
which framing they are using rather than blending the two, since "at goal" means different things
under each.

[4] (guideline-type-2-diabetes-first-line-therapy)
## The shape of current guidance

Older guidance set out a single sequence: metformin first, then agents added in order as control
worsened. Current guidance is structured differently — the first-line choice depends on which other
conditions are present, and for several of them the choice is made independently of the HbA1c value.
This is the substantive change, and it is the part most often stated in the old form.

## Where there is no compelling comorbidity

Metformin, alongside structured lifestyle intervention, is the usual initial agent: long experience,
low cost, weight neutrality, and little risk of causing low blood sugar on its own. Kidney function
is checked before starting and periodically after, since the dose is constrained below a threshold
of kidney function and the agent is avoided below a lower one. Gastrointestinal intolerance is the
common reason for stopping, and is reduced by gradual escalation and extended-release formulations.
Long-term use is associated with lower vitamin B12 levels, so periodic measurement is advised.

## Where cardiovascular, kidney or heart-failure disease is present

Guidance describes agents with demonstrated organ benefit as preferred, whether or not metformin is
also used, and independent of whether the HbA1c is at goal:

- **Established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease** — a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven
  cardiovascular benefit, or an SGLT-2 inhibitor with proven cardiovascular benefit.
- **Heart failure**, particularly with reduced ejection fraction — an SGLT-2 inhibitor.
- **Chronic kidney disease**, particularly with albuminuria — an SGLT-2 inhibitor, with a GLP-1
  receptor agonist as the alternative where an SGLT-2 inhibitor is not tolerated or not appropriate.

These are organ-protective therapies that also lower glucose, rather than later steps in a glucose
ladder. Class-specific cautions are part of the choice: SGLT-2 inhibitors carry a risk of genital
mycotic infection, volume depletion, and — uncommonly — ketoacidosis at near-normal glucose levels,
which is easy to miss precisely because the glucose is not high.

## Where weight is a major treatment goal

Agents with the greatest weight-reduction effect — the GLP-1 receptor agonists and dual incretin
agonists — are preferred where weight management is a primary objective, alongside structured
lifestyle intervention and, in selected people, metabolic surgery.

## Reassessment

The regimen is reviewed every three to six months. De-intensification is an explicit option, not a
failure: where the regimen has become more aggressive than the individualized target requires, or
where low blood sugar is occurring, stepping down is the appropriate response.

Doses, titration schedules and prescription decisions are outside the scope of this note and of this
system.

[5] (guideline-coronary-artery-disease-secondary-prevention)
## What secondary prevention means

Secondary prevention is the set of measures used for someone who already has established coronary
artery disease — a previous heart attack, a revascularization procedure, or angiographic disease —
to reduce the chance of a further event. It is a package rather than a single intervention: no one
element carries the effect, and the benefit measured in trials comes from applying them together.
Partial application is the common failure, and it is usually the non-drug elements that are dropped.

## The components

- **Antiplatelet therapy** — long-term single antiplatelet therapy for most people, with a defined
  period of dual antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome or stent placement, its
  duration individualized against bleeding risk.
- **High-intensity statin therapy**. United States guidance describes the intensity; European
  guidance describes an LDL goal instead. Where the response is inadequate, additional
  non-statin agents are added rather than the statin abandoned.
- **Blood-pressure control**, with a target below 130/80 mm Hg for most people.
- **Renin-angiotensin blockade** where diabetes, reduced left ventricular function, or chronic
  kidney disease is also present.
- **Beta-blockade** after myocardial infarction, with the strongest and longest-standing evidence
  where left ventricular function is reduced.
- **Cardiac rehabilitation referral** — a structured program of supervised exercise, education and
  risk-factor management, and consistently one of the most underused elements relative to the
  strength of the evidence behind it.
- **Smoking cessation**, the single largest modifiable factor, with combined behavioral and
  pharmacologic support more effective than advice alone.
- **Annual influenza vaccination**, included as a cardiovascular measure rather than only a
  respiratory one.
- **Structured management of diabetes** where present, preferring agents with demonstrated
  cardiovascular benefit.

## Review interval

Review at least annually once the regimen is stable, with earlier review after any change in
symptoms, after a hospital admission, and four to twelve weeks after any change in lipid-lowering
intensity. Each review is an opportunity to check adherence, which falls measurably in the year
after an event as the acute experience recedes.

## What warrants urgent reassessment

New, worsening, or rest-onset chest discomfort in someone with known coronary disease is not a
routine review matter and requires urgent assessment. A pattern of angina that is becoming more
frequent, more easily provoked, or longer-lasting is a change in category rather than a change in
degree. The emergency-symptom notes elsewhere in this corpus govern these situations, and this note
does not substitute for them.

question: Why does low iron make people tired?
answer:
Low iron levels can lead to fatigue primarily through a condition known as iron-deficiency anemia. Iron is essential for producing hemoglobin, the component of red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body. When there is not enough iron, the production of hemoglobin decreases. This reduction means that less oxygen is delivered to tissues and organs, which can result in feelings of tiredness and decreased exercise tolerance.

Common symptoms associated with low iron levels include fatigue, breathlessness with exertion, and a reduced ability to perform physical activities. As the body struggles to meet its oxygen needs, people may also experience palpitations, headaches, and dizziness. Many individuals may not notice these symptoms initially, often attributing their fatigue to life circumstances, and may present for evaluation only when symptoms become more severe (source: General clinical reference on iron-deficiency anemia). 

If someone is experiencing significant fatigue or related symptoms, discussing these with a healthcare provider can help determine the underlying cause and appropriate next steps.
